Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

Industry observers note that “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell states. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

It has been revealed that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

It has been revealed that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Industry observers note that yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Industry observers note that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

In a recent development, if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Recent findings suggest that sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

It has been revealed that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga indicates. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Latest York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

According to recent reports, but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Recent findings suggest that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics firm XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” indicates Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Industry observers note that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson indicates. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

It has been revealed that after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell states. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” states neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

It has been revealed that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

In a recent development, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu notes.

It has been revealed that medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” states neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Recent findings suggest that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra claims, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

According to recent reports, if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

Recent findings suggest that in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

According to recent reports, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

Industry observers note that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy declared US $62 million in newly introduced funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga states they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How rapidly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print matter as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

Booking.com’s Marnie Wilking says AI can chain old bugs into fraud

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Booking.com chief security officer Marnie Wilking (left) and TNW’s Cristian Dina at Web Summit in Lisbon, 12 November 2026.
  • Sources indicate that AI can now chain old bugs in a platform’s code into an attack, Booking.com’s Marnie Wilking told TNW.
  • “AI can find those and then figure out how to chain multiple of those together to actually find its way through the system or figure out how to perpetrate fraud on your platform.” Marnie Wilking, Booking.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Booking.com chief security officer Marnie Wilking (left) and TNW’s Cristian Dina at Web Summit in Lisbon, 12 November 2026.

Sources indicate that AI can now chain old bugs in a platform’s code into an attack, Booking.com’s Marnie Wilking told TNW. Some of those flaws may have sat unnoticed for five or 10 years, she said. Companies now have to go back, find them and fix them.

“AI can find those and then figure out how to chain multiple of those together to actually find its way through the system or figure out how to perpetrate fraud on your platform.” Marnie Wilking, Booking.com.

Recent findings suggest that wilking is Booking.com’s chief security officer, responsible for cybersecurity, fraud, trust and safety, and corporate security. She joined four years ago as chief information security officer.

Sources indicate that she spoke to Cristian Dina for the TNW Podcast at Web Summit in Lisbon, her first time at the event. Earlier episodes featured Ronan Harris of Snap, Danila Shtan of Nebius, and Alexander Rinke of Celonis. The full conversation is in the video below.

Attacks on travel and hospitality ramped up after the pandemic, Wilking said. People rushed to travel again, and attackers saw the money in it. ChatGPT’s release in November 2022 gave them AI. They can now send phishing messages at scale, in many languages, with flawless grammar and personal details.

Attackers may not have real booking details, she said. They can guess, or pick up hints from social media posts, such as a trip to Lisbon. They also go after hotels and other partners directly, stealing logins on Booking.com or at the hotel. Some steal travellers’ logins to make fake bookings, which they then use to attack partners.

It has been revealed that booking.com now requires two-factor authentication for partners and for guests, Wilking said. Machine learning checks whether a login looks normal: the same phone, browser and IP address. If something looks off, the platform can ask for extra steps, such as entering card details again before a payment.

According to recent reports, as those controls cut attacks on Booking.com’s own platform, attackers turned to the wider ecosystem, she stated. Targets include property management systems and travel agencies. Attackers also hit the connectivity providers that sync a property’s calendar across Booking.com, Airbnb and Vrbo.

In a recent development, booking.com shares threat intelligence through the Retail and Hospitality Information Sharing and Analysis Center (RH-ISAC). Some of its competitors and partners are members too. Members share upcoming threats, not competitive information. One recent scam shared there flipped the usual threat of a cancelled booking.

“Oh, you paid us too much. Click on this link and give us your credit card details so we can give you a refund.” Marnie Wilking, Booking.com, on a scam message sent to guests.

Smaller hotels often have no security team. Booking.com runs security and fraud sessions for its partners at events in Amsterdam, Asia Pacific and the Americas. Its approach has three parts, she said: prevent attacks, detect and respond swiftly, and educate people.

Booking.com’s security team uses AI to scan its code repositories and external endpoints for flaws. Many are not security vulnerabilities in the traditional sense, Wilking mentioned. They are bugs and business logic flaws that AI can chain together. She called it a cat-and-mouse game over who finds them first.

Sources indicate that she compared AI to the internet in the late 1990s, then the mobile and cloud shifts, each faster than the last. Asked whether AI development should slow down, she said attackers will keep using it either way.

“Whether we choose as a society to say we’d like to slow this down, the bad guys are not going to slow down.” Marnie Wilking, Booking.com.

Booking.com already has an AI trip planner, and is looking at AI for travel inspiration. Her team works with product teams on security, privacy, and trust and safety, she said, because AI can hallucinate. It must not invent a hotel or sell attraction tickets that are not real.

Wilking studied maths. A Big Four consulting firm then recruited her for IT work at a big bank. She spent many years at Wells Fargo, ending as security officer for its mortgage division. She then moved to a smaller financial services company that worked in the cloud, became chief information security officer at a healthcare technology company based in Auckland, and later held the same role at Wayfair.

Industry observers note that her advice to travellers: use multi-factor authentication and a password manager, and be suspicious of anything that does not look right. If a message appears to come from a hotel, call the hotel directly.

  • This shift changes how devices are designed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

Among iOS 27’s many new features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces big AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting latest features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the patch also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

Industry observers note that after iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

Industry observers note that to move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most consumers will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

Industry observers note that I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple looks to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

In a recent development, do you have a need to use the same phone number on multiple iPhones? For what reason? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for most people, dictation is far easier and quicker than typing, which raises the question: why do we still spend so much time typing out emails and documents? Often, it's because opening and setting up dictation software takes too long when you just need to get a note down promptly. SecondBrain’s VoicePad promises to be something quite different: An AI-powered dictation device that works even when you whisper, and gives you one-touch buttons for quick app launching.

It’s the ultimate desk companion.

Industry observers note that the SecondBrain VoicePad is a CNC-machined, small, lightweight handheld device with five individual customizable buttons and dual microphones that can pick up your voice in loud environments or when you’re whispering. It’s highly portable, so you can carry it around with you for easy access to your most crucial apps, and to take notes and dictation whenever you need it, without all the usual “ums” and false-starts that make dictated notes so hard to read.

Workers brainstorming on a commute can take down a few key notes, or have the device’s AI whip them up into a first-draft report. Remote creators can easily record some ideas for their novel, Dungeons and Dragons campaign, or their next musical composition. Software developers who just had a flash of inspiration can flesh out the idea by triggering the VoicePad’s AI to expand on their original thought.

It has been revealed that you can use the VoicePad for longer-form content, too, and replace the need to type almost entirely. Dictate emails, chapters of your book, or wholesale reports. With SecondBrain VoicePad, anyone can dictate at up to 160 words per minute, making it one of the fastest ways to record information accurately and effectively.

It works in any app with a text input box, too, so whatever you’re doing with words, the VoicePad can help you get them down clearly for later reading, or AI analysis and extrapolation.

You can also fully customize the VoicePad. The default configuration gives you quick access to your Calendar and AI apps, but you can remap each button to launch whatever apps you find most useful. You can rapidly pull up your email, image editing app, web browser or whatever you like with the tap of a button.

Dictation is often difficult in busy areas where there are lots of background noise, and in particularly quiet ones, where you can’t speak loud enough to be heard effectively. The SecondBrain VoicePad is built to work wherever you are and however you say it. Its dual microphones will pick up your voice even if you’re whispering, and they can pick you out from the crowd of background noise, too. That means you can take notes anywhere, whether you’re in a silent library or a busy airport terminal.

Only your voice and that of any colleagues present will be recorded, delivering clear written results, including names, numbers, and mixed languages. This is particularly useful when recording meetings between departments or across time zones, where different language preferences can make following along difficult. With the SecondBrain VoicePad you can feel confident that you didn’t miss anything in the meeting, with after-action AI minutes and notes making it easier to digest what was stated.

Most dictation devices need a laptop connection, too. Not the SecondBrain VoicePad. With 20 hours of battery life, you can carry this independent dictation device with you and rest assured it’s always ready to record what you need; No additional devices necessary.

The VoicePad is designed to enhance the dictation experience with Genspark AI. If you’re already on Genspark, the VoicePad can act like your AI workspace right out of the box. Just tap the button and you’re off and running. Ask it to make a slideshow from your notes, create a full report, or bounce ideas back and forth with you. One dictated note can generate whole range of of alternatives for you to consider - fantastic for off-the-cuff ideation.

According to recent reports, if you already use cloud-based AI solutions like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Grok, you can link those with your VoicePad so all your AI requests are routed through those accounts instead. If you use multiples of them, you can even give each AI agent its own button, so you can send your dictated notes to the right one.

Recent findings suggest that not into AI? Don’t sweat it. SecondBrain VoicePad works just as well as a standalone dictation device and app launcher. It means leaving the AI features and support on the tablel, but even then the VoicePad isl fantastic for dictating emails, recording meetings, and translating international languages into something you can readily understand.

The SecondBrain VoicePad is now crowdfunding on Kickstarter with the campaign running through December. Super-Early adopters can get a SecondBrain VoicePad for just $119 - that’s $50 off its retail price of $169.

Each pledge comes with the VoicePad itself, with five customizable buttons, and unlimited real-time voice input, so you can record your voice with no additional cost. You get a year of unlimited dictation support, too, with 4,000 words a week free after that. Genspark Plus, Pro, and Team members can continue to enjoy unlimited voice typing and a free pool of tokens to use each day for transcription services.

Every SecondBrain VoicePad buyer gets unlimited translation service for the first year, too, making it ideal for multi-language meetings or travelling abroad with added confidence. After that 12-month period, translations cost a single credit per minute, but with Genspark credits priced at $25 for 10,000 a month, you’re unlikely to run out anytime soon.

The SecondBrain VoicePad is set to begin shipping in January to pledgees all over the world.

Figma engineer sues over the company’s harassment complaint process

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Figma engineer is suing the design software tech giant and its CEO, Dylan Field, saying her harassment complaints were met with orders to face the colleagues she accused.
  • Recent findings suggest that serry Park, who still works at Figma, filed the case in federal court in Fresh York on Monday.
  • According to recent reports, we have reviewed the 61-page complaint, and its claims have not been tested in court.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Figma engineer is suing the design software tech giant and its CEO, Dylan Field, saying her harassment complaints were met with orders to face the colleagues she accused. TechCrunch, which interviewed her before the filing, first reported the suit.

Recent findings suggest that serry Park, who still works at Figma, filed the case in federal court in Fresh York on Monday. In the complaint, she claims sexual harassment, retaliation, and discrimination based on race, gender, and sexual orientation, and accuses Field personally of aiding and abetting under New York law.

According to recent reports, we have reviewed the 61-page complaint, and its claims have not been tested in court. Yet, her performance reviews, the suit says, leaned on stereotypes about Asian women.

“Figma has a sexual harassment problem,” the complaint opens, arguing that Field has done nothing to fix it.

The complaint’s central charge is about process. Figma’s culture of direct feedback, it alleges, meant that managers and HR repeatedly sent Park back to face the people she had accused, rather than looking into her complaints.

The suit describes a pattern across two teams and several years. Also, an early mentor allegedly kept pursuing Park after she turned down a date, behaviour the complaint describes as stalking and unwanted sexual advances. Managers twice refused her requests to be separated from him, and one put him on a project she led.

Industry observers note that years later, on a different team, a manager allegedly made comments about her sex life at a team lunch. HR closed that investigation without speaking to witnesses, the suit says.

Low reviews and a reduced bonus followed her complaints, according to the filing, while men in similar positions advanced. Park took medical leave this March and was cleared to return in June with changes to her schedule, which she says were approved but never put in place.

The filing insists this was policy, not a few rogue managers. Two different managers, her lead People Partner and Figma’s HR team, gave Park the same instruction, it states, across three years, two teams, and two different accused colleagues.

The suit works to pin that culture on Field himself. He picked Figma’s values, including one telling staff to share direct feedback, and signed the annual report publishing them, the complaint notes.

Citing Figma’s own proxy statement, it adds that Field controls 72.3% of the voting power, making Figma a controlled organization under stock-exchange rules.

According to recent reports, the pressure allegedly continued once lawyers got involved. Days after Figma learned in July that Park intended to sue, a supervisor asked her to switch teams again. The suit casts that as fresh retaliation, resetting her career a second time and pulling her away from her speciality.

According to recent reports, park wants damages and a jury trial, and she also wants the court to bar Figma from making staff who report harassment face the accused, and to order a prompt, confidential complaints process. The suit asks too that she be placed in the senior role she says she was denied.

“These claims have no merit, and we will present the facts in court,” a Figma spokesperson told TechCrunch.

The spokesperson added that Figma does not tolerate discrimination, harassment, or extortion.

The case comes while Figma defends a separate proposed class action in California, filed last November, over claims it trained AI models on customers’ design files without consent, which Figma has moved to dismiss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you picked up a newly introduced iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started. We’ve got you covered with some great deals on premium accessories for nearly every Apple device on your list.

It has been revealed that ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile. Here’s a look at what’s included in ESR’s Black Friday lineup and who each one is for.

According to recent reports, if someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right. As we’ve seen with Android foldables, you’re protecting two halves, a hinge, and a phone that changes shape throughout the day as you use it, all without adding bulk to a device people bought because it folds thin. ESR has two options for iPhone Duo owners, and the choice mostly comes down to the look you want to achieve.

The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand is your choice if you want to show off your iPhone Duo’s colors. It combines a rigid polycarbonate and acrylic back with a softer TPU frame. The rigid back keeps the case from flexing and lets the iPhone Duo’s design show through, while the flexible frame absorbs the shock if you drop it (please don’t).

The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. It’s made from organic silicone leather with a soft, skin-friendly feel and a stain-resistant finish. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually demonstrates every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

Both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR notes it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

According to recent reports, both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

In a recent development, the same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

On these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

Protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case is up to 28% off, and the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case is up to 37% off.

A case protects everything except the part you touch all day. The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the name is worth unpacking. Armorite is ESR’s line of toughened screen protectors, and the Pro version is made with Accessory Glass by Corning™. Corning has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone, so in non-tech speak, this is glass from a trustworthy name rather than generic tempered glass.

Sources indicate that why it matters: ESR says the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing shows up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

Recent findings suggest that installation is the part most people dread on a brand-upcoming iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Black Friday deal: The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector is 15% off.

Holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and noted it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

Sources indicate that it’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR indicates it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to 50% in about 15 minutes. It’s also TÜV-certified, meaning an independent testing organization has verified its safety features.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger is up to 32% off from November 20 through December 1.

Recent findings suggest that for the student or anyone who does real work on an iPad, the ESR Shift Keyboard Case makes for an incredible gift. The Bluetooth keyboard attaches magnetically and comes off when you don’t need it, so you can type an essay at a desk, then pull the keyboard away to watch something on the couch or sketch with the iPad flat on a table.

According to recent reports, ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

The trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

The ESR Shift Keyboard Case comes in versions for iPad Pro 11-inch and 13-inch (M4 and M5), iPad Air 11-inch and 13-inch (including the upcoming M4 models), and iPad (A16), so whichever iPad you’re trying to take to the next level of productivity, there’s a Shift that fits it.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Shift Keyboard Case is up to 25% off, depending on your iPad model.

According to recent reports, have you ever dropped your AirPods case and watched the earbuds go flying? With the Cyber FlickLock, you won’t have to worry about that. We’ve covered FlickLock in MagSafe Monday before, but let’s recap it.

When the internal latch is engaged, the magnets line up to attract each other and hold the lid shut with maximum force, adding a second layer of security. Slide the button, and the magnets shift to repel each other, so the lid pops open with one hand. ESR notes the slide mechanism has been tested over 20,000 times.

The result is that your AirPods stay in the case if you drop it. Both cases also have 260g of magnetic strength, so they snap onto MagSafe chargers, Apple Watch chargers, and MagSafe batteries if you need to charge your AirPods. Again, it’s extremely strong, but extremely easy to unlock with one hand.

Recent findings suggest that the ESR Cyber FlickLock Magnetic Case is extremely durable and has a clip hook, so you can hang your AirPods on a backpack while hiking or cycling. The ESR Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Case brings the same lock in a range of vibrant colors with a carrying lanyard, so you can wear your AirPods on your wrist or attach them to a bag. Both cases come in versions for AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2 and 1, and AirPods 5 and 4. No matter which AirPods you or your loved one have, this is the case everyone will love.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Cyber FlickLock and Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Cases are both 20% off.

Recent findings suggest that the ESR Equinox Watch Band is a quick pick for anyone who works out in the morning while tracking progress with Apple Watch, then heads to the office. A pin-and-fold lock keeps it secure, and it’s made from HNBR, a durable, skin-friendly synthetic rubber that resists water and tearing, with ventilation cutouts for all-day comfort. It fits 44mm, 45mm, 46mm, and 49mm models across Apple Watch Ultra 1 through 4, Series 4 through 12, and SE 1 through 3, and it comes in several colors to match your outfit or your mood that day.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Equinox Watch Band is 20% off.

According to recent reports, the best gifts are the ones that get used every day, and accessories are the part of the Apple experience people live with the most. A case that props up a foldable, a screen protector made with Corning glass, a charger with a built-in cable, and an AirPods case that stays closed even when dropped check all the boxes. ESR truly makes something for everyone and is one of the most trusted names in the Apple accessories ecosystem.

In a recent development, ESR built its Black Friday lineup around the whole Apple ecosystem, from the upcoming iPhone Duo to iPad, AirPods, and even a great Apple Watch band, with premium materials and versatile designs that are durable, functional, and great-looking. ESR’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals run on Amazon from November 19 through November 30 (the Xtend 45W runs through December 1), with discounts of up to 37%!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. If you ask any Mac admin for a list of the software on their fleet, they’ll pull up their device management inventory and show you the apps they’ve deployed. Ask them what their developers installed with Homebrew last month, which VS Code extensions they are running, or what npm pulled into a project on Tuesday, and you’ll get a different response. That software was never procured by finance, never approved, and never inventoried. It’s also where a growing share of the risk lives in the AI era. Workbrew 2.0 treats that gap as a problem worth solving for IT teams.

Recent findings suggest that about Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train customers, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Industry observers note that device management is built around the software IT deploys. Apps from Apple Business Manager, apps preloaded via your device management vendors’ packages, packages you upload, and profiles you push out. That model solves the problem for native macOS apps. It doesn’t cover what happens when the Mac becomes the default developer machine. Developers install what they need with a single command in Terminal, and Homebrew alone has more than 16,000 packages. You then add millions of npm packages and hundreds of thousands of IDE extensions, and the list of software on a Mac that IT didn’t put there is longer than the list it did.

That used to be a developer-only problem. It isn’t anymore, in the vibe-coding era. AI tools have turned marketers, analysts, and ops people into builders, and those builders install packages too.

Workbrew started as a management layer for Homebrew: an agent that reports what’s installed, flags known vulnerabilities, and lets IT push updates across the fleet. Version 2.0 expands the catalog to include npm packages, VS Code extensions, and macOS apps, all in a single inventory. The manufacturer says it has patched more than 10 million vulnerabilities for customers since its launch, and it’s now ISO 27001-certified.

It has been revealed that the part that is critical for everyone who isn’t a developer is the newly introduced Workbrew app, a native Mac app for finding, installing, and updating approved software. Workbrew calls it “the app store for your entire company.” Employees can browse what IT has approved, install it without opening Terminal, and request anything that isn’t on the list. IT approves or denies in the Workbrew Console, and if it’s a no, the employee gets an answer on why.

The app comes from the Updatest team, which Workbrew acquired as part of this release. Updatest is the indie Mac app that keeps thousands of owners’ software up to date, and it remains a separate product for individuals and families. For business customer, that experience is now the Workbrew app, and it’s included on every proposal, including the free Team plan with no device or user limits.

Recent findings suggest that with Workbrew, we finally have real visibility into what developers are using in Homebrew. Fleet-wide updates are effortless, and the team stays secure without being slowed down.

Chris Merrell, Director of IT, End User Services, Camping World.

According to recent reports, workbrew isn’t a device management tool and isn’t trying to be one. Your device management system deploys the Workbrew agent, and Workbrew handles software your device management system lacks visibility into. If your fleet consists entirely of office workers on managed apps, there’s nothing here for you. If you have developers, or you’ve noticed the marketing team installing things to run AI scripts, you have the problem whether you’ve discovered it or not.

Sources indicate that AI tools have changed how we think about app management, because apps get installed differently now. Workbrew 2.0 provides IT with a list of development tools on the Mac and gives employees a sanctioned way to get what they need.

#165534. Latest Update: AI is ruining apps. Pavlo Razumovskyi is betting it can save them too

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1311 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: AI is ruining apps. Pavlo Razumovskyi is betting it can save them too

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if your favorite app’s home screen feels clunkier, slower and more generic than it did a few years ago, Pavlo Razumovskyi claims you’re not imagining it.
  • Sources indicate that razumovskyi is co-founder and vice president of engineering at Coframe, a San Francisco tech giant backed by Khosla Ventures that builds what it calls living interfaces: apps, websites, emails and chat experiences that adapt to each visitor instead of showing everyone the same thing.
  • AI coding tools have made shipping a feature cheap, and that has changed the question product teams ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pavlo Razumovskyi, co-founder of Coframe.

In a recent development, if your favorite app’s home screen feels clunkier, slower and more generic than it did a few years ago, Pavlo Razumovskyi claims you’re not imagining it. He calls it enshittification of the interface, borrowing the term the writer Cory Doctorow coined for platforms that decay as they grow. And he thinks AI is both the cause and the cure.

Sources indicate that razumovskyi is co-founder and vice president of engineering at Coframe, a San Francisco tech giant backed by Khosla Ventures that builds what it calls living interfaces: apps, websites, emails and chat experiences that adapt to each visitor instead of showing everyone the same thing. Before that he was a staff machine learning engineer at Pinterest, and before that co-founder and chief technology officer of InkHunter, a tattoo try-on app that passed 20 million downloads and was later sold to private equity.

AI coding tools have made shipping a feature cheap, and that has changed the question product teams ask.

“Teams used to ask, who is this for and why should we build it,” he remarked. “Now the question is, why not vibe-ship it and see what it does to the metrics. That is how you end up with the most confusing products the industry has ever designed.”.

Sources indicate that the deeper problem, in his view, is that almost every product is built with one page for everyone. Dynamic feeds personalize the content, but the interface around the feed stays fixed. Every team adds a feature, a feed, a product line. Past a certain point the product is too complex for anyone, and no amount of optimization brings the simplicity back.

Razumovskyi has spent a decade designing machine learning into the way people interact with screens. His conclusion is that the same generative AI that lets teams ship clutter faster can also be the foundation for experiences that are personal and considered.

Sources indicate that the idea has a long history in his own work. It starts at a 48-hour hackathon in Ukraine in 2014, where a student team built a demo that let you point a phone at your arm and see a tattoo on it.

Razumovskyi and Oleksandra Rohachova turned the demo into InkHunter in January 2015. He was co-founder and chief technology officer, and he wrote the technology himself: a proprietary skin-tracking engine that ran in real time on a phone and blended a design into skin convincingly enough that people trusted it for a permanent decision. It took a year to build and launch. The app passed 1 million downloads in its first year on the market.

“Pavlo built the tracking engine and most of the product code,” Rohachova stated. “We got into Y Combinator on the strength of what he had built, and every product we shipped after that ran on that code.”.

It has been revealed that the founders moved to the United States as the app grew. Apple named InkHunter one of the best apps of 2017, Y Combinator accepted the tech giant into its summer 2018 batch, and across its apps InkHunter passed 20 million downloads. Razumovskyi extended the engine into markerless hand tracking for a jewelry try-on, then built a marketplace and booking system that connected owners with hundreds of tattoo artists. The business turned profitable. InkHunter was later sold to private equity.

The key insight hasn’t changed since day one. Don’t show someone else’s tattoo. Show the tattoo on the user’s own body. Make it unique, make it relevant, and make the decision easier.

Sources indicate that in 2021 he joined Pinterest’s Advanced Technology Group, the team charged with getting new technology into production, as a staff machine learning engineer and tech lead under Charles Rosenberg, who heads the group and previously led image search at Google. The problems were bigger versions of the one he had solved before. He worked on virtual try-on for makeup, fashion and furniture, using augmented reality, 3D and diffusion models, and on visual search and ad personalization. He also led the group’s early experiments in generating interfaces with large language models.

“I first noticed Pavlo because of InkHunter. He had solved a hard computer vision problem on a phone with a tiny team,” Rosenberg said. “At Pinterest he did the same thing at a different scale. He was exploring AI-generated interfaces and generated ad creatives while most of the industry was still talking about chatbots.”.

The job also put him between two cultures. Machine learning teams ranked every piece of content per user and thought in embeddings and loss functions. Product and design teams thought in user journeys, jobs to be done and product metrics.

Industry observers note that “There is no perfect interface for every person in every situation,” Razumovskyi said. “Once you accept that, the answer is obvious. Generate interfaces and rank them the way you rank content. Real customers in a specific moment need different tools, different messages, different experiences. AI should not be used to generate yet another screen. It should generate the screen for this user, right now.”.

In November 2023 he co-founded Coframe with Josh Payne.

In a recent development, the manufacturer does one thing. It generates, tests and refines versions of a customer’s web pages so that each visitor gets the interface most likely to work for them, and it keeps doing it as behavior changes. An AI system can pay attention to every user journey, remember past interactions and adapt on the fly in a way no product team can.

Razumovskyi designed the platform’s core architecture: the engine that generates page variants, the personalization layer that decides who sees which one, and the analytics that measure the result.

It has been revealed that in 2024 Coframe worked with OpenAI’s vision fine-tuning team to train a version of GPT-4o that generates on-brand interface code from a single prompt, and built a benchmark, BrandBench, to score how closely generated sections match a site’s existing design. OpenAI featured the work when it debuted vision fine-tuning. Razumovskyi led Coframe’s engineering on the project.

Sources indicate that “Pavlo owns the architecture and the roadmap. If it touches production, he designed how it works,” Payne said. “When a new opportunity shows up, he’s the one who makes it work.”.

In a recent development, khosla Ventures has backed Coframe since its first round. It co-led the $9.3 million seed in October 2024 and, in November 2026, the $25 million Series A that brought total funding to $35 million. The firm now works with upper mid-market and enterprise customers including Replit, Dropbox, Cash App and TUI, one of the world’s largest travel companies. In the 18 months since its commercial launch it has grown from no revenue to more than $6 million in annual recurring revenue, and it claims its optimization has generated more than $300 million in incremental revenue for customers.

The customers describe the change in blunt terms.

Sources indicate that “The old way was really hard,” stated Alex Lin, a growth marketer at Replit. “Coframe enables the idea-to-optimization cycle faster than most people would ever think is possible.”.

Alexey Komissarouk, head of growth engineering at Anthropic, put it more briefly in a testimonial on Coframe’s site: “In a world full of AI vaporware, Coframe is for real.”.

For Razumovskyi it comes back to the lesson from the tattoo app.

Industry observers note that “Don’t show your product in the abstract,” he stated. “Show it in the context of the customer’s actual problem. Make it unique, make it relevant, and make the decision easier.”.

In a recent development, whether you’re a solopreneur or a small business owner, Google Workspace offers enterprise-grade capabilities that include custom email domains, centralized administration, and fully scalable storage and support. Three main tiers are available, with the flexibility to upgrade as your business grows:.

Recent findings suggest that business Starter includes Gemini assistance in Gmail and the standalone Gemini Chat app. In-depth assistance within other Google apps requires Business Standard or higher.

Gemini in Gmail and Google Docs can help you create compelling sales and marketing copy across all channels: brochures, web copy, sales pitches, proposals, blog posts, social media, customer emails, and more.

Gemini can also bring your marketing campaigns to life with eye-catching imagery. A simple prompt is all you need to generate editable slides and visuals.

Gemini takes you from blank page to brilliance by generating fully-formatted first drafts of all your promotional materials without countless hours of work or expensive external consultants.

You can create polished sales and marketing videos in minutes with Google Vids by using Gemini to transform static product images into high-quality animations.

Industry observers note that with Gemini Omni included in Google Vids, you can even create videos using your personal avatar. Text-to-speech capabilities provide AI voiceovers and avatar narration with natural-sounding inflections, pacing, and context-aware emphasis.

If you’ve ever wished you had an administrative assistant with you during video calls for sales pitches and client meeting, Gemini in Meet can take notes for you and then automatically generate summaries and action points.

Industry observers note that for businesses that work internationally, Gemini in Meet can also break down language barriers, translating speech in real time – with translated captions for 60+ languages. Gemini in Sheets can act as a business analyst and researcher, helping you carry out tasks like building cash flow models, creating project schedules, and pulling together competitive research tables.

Gemini can identify the external data you need and automatically paste the figures directly into Google Sheets documents. If you want to dig deeper into any of the data, Gemini provides the exact web sources used for each individual cell.

For tasks like summarizing, categorizing, and processing internal business data, Gemini assistance lets you carry out this work up to 55 times faster than manual entry based on a 500-cell task.

You can even create custom mini apps in Sheets just by using simple prompts.

According to recent reports, no business can risk client or internal business data leaking into public AI models. Google Workspace Privacy Hub ensures that all your interactions with Gemini remain completely confidential.

Your content is never used for AI training or subject to human review unless you choose to grant permission.

A single subscription combines the complete Google Workspace productivity suite and Gemini AI capabilities (Gmail and standalone app with Business Starter, the full set of AI tools with all other tiers).

Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming in 2027

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner.
  • It has been revealed that 2027 is going to be a relatively substantial iPhone release year for Apple.
  • For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

It has been revealed that 2027 is going to be a relatively substantial iPhone release year for Apple. First, the firm will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a new round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will revision the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 currently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

Recent findings suggest that this phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too notable – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It has been revealed that it should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

Industry observers note that for the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

It has been revealed that I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

It has been revealed that lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-declared iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.
