  • I’m always on the lookout for something upcoming to add to my Netflix watchlist, especially when there’s a good mix of psychological thrillers, gripping dramas and a little bit of horror.
  • According to recent reports, thankfully, the streamer’s latest top 10 list has a few titles that have caught my attention, including one particularly twisted psychological drama that feels like “Mean Girls” meets “Jennifer's Body,” with a little bit of “Carrie” thrown in for good measure.
  • It has been revealed that leading the way is a provocative teen drama about a group of Catholic schoolgirls whose spooky initiation takes a disturbing turn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m always on the lookout for something upcoming to add to my Netflix watchlist, especially when there’s a good mix of psychological thrillers, gripping dramas and a little bit of horror.

According to recent reports, thankfully, the streamer’s latest top 10 list has a few titles that have caught my attention, including one particularly twisted psychological drama that feels like “Mean Girls” meets “Jennifer's Body,” with a little bit of “Carrie” thrown in for good measure. If you’re anything like me and enjoy discovering your next binge-watch, these three reveals deserve a closer look.

It has been revealed that leading the way is a provocative teen drama about a group of Catholic schoolgirls whose spooky initiation takes a disturbing turn. There’s also a gripping limited series inspired by one of the biggest financial scandals in recent history, following two ambitious young entrepreneurs whose relationship and business empire spiral out of control.

Finally, a lavish historical drama returns for its third and final season, with complicated relationships and plenty of royal scheming.

Note: This list is based on the Netflix U.S. top 10 highlights as of Tuesday, November 24, 2026.

Netflix’s current No. 1 show is “The Body,” a coming-of-age psychological drama that’s perfect if you enjoy your teen stories with a much darker edge. It’s been compared to “Mean Girls” meets “Jennifer’s Body,” with shades of “Carrie” and “Yellowjackets” thrown in.

In a recent development, creator Quinn Shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell have also drawn on their own high school experiences and religious upbringing to give the story a more personal feel. It basically thrives on early 2000s nostalgia, which leans into what Shephard calls “gritty camp.” It’s a raunchy, unsettling teen drama, and certainly a little different from your usual coming-of-age stories.

Industry observers note that “The Body” follows a group of students at an elite Catholic school whose lives take a disturbing turn after a Halloween party goes wrong. When the school’s all-girls dance team welcomes a new recruit, the group marks the occasion with an outrageous initiation ritual.

In a recent development, however, their night takes an unexpected turn when fellow student Grace (Sofia Wylie) falls into a coma. Anxious to avoid getting into trouble, the girls agree to keep what happened a secret. But when students begin reporting strange visions of Grace, rumors spread throughout the wider community, leaving the girls struggling to explain what they witnessed.

Sources indicate that “The Altruists” is presently competing for the No. 1 spot on Netflix, and it’s easy to see why this real-life financial scandal makes for such compelling viewing. The biographical drama follows the rise and spectacular collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX, focusing on co-founders Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison.

It has been revealed that their relationship takes centre stage as an $8 billion fraud scandal sends shockwaves through the financial world. The show actually draws on public reporting, court transcripts and financial journalism to piece together the events surrounding FTX’s downfall. Fans of “The Dropout” and “Inventing Anna” should definitely have this one on their watchlist.

Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner) are two ambitious young entrepreneurs who set out to transform the global financial industry. After meeting in New York, the pair develop a romantic relationship while building their respective cryptocurrency businesses, with Sam at the helm of exchange FTX and Caroline running trading firm Alameda Research.

Recent findings suggest that as their companies attract billions of dollars in investments, their growing empire brings them extraordinary wealth and influence. However, behind the scenes, questionable business decisions and mounting financial problems threaten everything they’ve built.

Stream "The Altruists" on Netflix.

Finally, “The Empress” is another great Netflix historical drama to add to your watchlist, particularly if you enjoy lavish period pieces like “The Crown” and “Bridgerton.” This International Emmy-winning German series follows the life of Empress Elisabeth of Austria, with plenty of romance and bold costumes along the way.

The good news for fans is that season 3 was always planned as the final chapter, rather than being cut short unexpectedly. Creator Katharina Eyssen wanted three seasons to tell a complete story with a proper beginning, middle and end, giving the series a chance to wrap up its characters’ journeys.

In a recent development, following the devastating Sardinian War, Emperor Franz (Philip Froissant) returns to Vienna a changed man, struggling with the loss of thousands of soldiers. His wife, Empress Elisabeth (Devrim Lingnau), tries to support him while fighting to save their fragile marriage.

However, Franz’s infidelity and growing tensions at court eventually drive Elisabeth to leave Vienna. During her journey, she meets Count Andrássy (Dejan Bućin), a Hungarian revolutionary who promptly captures her attention. Meanwhile, Franz’s brother Maximilian (Johannes Nussbaum) travels to Mexico to claim the imperial throne.

Stream "The Empress" 3 on Netflix.

Recent findings suggest that you likely have a TV on your wall that generally sits idle throughout the day. While the Apple TV does offer loads of built in screensavers, you might be looking for something a bit more artsy. Salon offers a picture frame experience for the Apple TV, where it has over 1000 open-access paintings to display.

Sources indicate that in short, this app replicates the Samsung Frame TV experience but for anyone who owns an Apple TV. As mentioned above, you can choose from over 1000 hand-picked art pieces to choose from the world’s museums, but you can also import your own photos from iCloud.

Salon lets you add a frame to the edge of your photos, or you can display them edge-to-edge if you’d like. You can also add a clock and date to the corner.

Here’s why the developer, Rene, decided to build Salon. If you’ve ever owned a Samsung Frame TV, you’ll likely resonate with the story:.

I bought a Samsung Frame a few years back and was pretty appalled by Tizen and the fact that they charge a subscription for the art mode. It annoyed me enough to build my own, at first just for my own TV. I also noticed that tvOS gets very little love from indie developers. Outside Apple’s own apps and the substantial streaming apps, it’s mostly aquariums and fireplaces. Although now with the whole vibe coding craze, there are a few more interesting additions as well.

According to recent reports, salon is available as a one time $9.99 purchase on the App Store for Apple TVs running tvOS 17 and later. For the 9to5Mac audience, we also have 4 promo codes for lucky readers to score a free copy:.

UK finance watchdog warns AI agent builders they may need a licence

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (483 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Britain’s financial watchdog has a message for companies building AI agents that handle people’s money: you may need its permission to operate.
  • The Financial Conduct Authority set out its expectations for agentic AI on Tuesday, covering banks, tech providers, and social media platforms alike.
  • Sources indicate that the regulator says companies are moving from testing AI agents to deploying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Britain’s financial watchdog has a message for companies building AI agents that handle people’s money: you may need its permission to operate.

The Financial Conduct Authority set out its expectations for agentic AI on Tuesday, covering banks, tech providers, and social media platforms alike.

Sources indicate that the regulator says companies are moving from testing AI agents to deploying them. It is already talking to companies planning personal AI agents for UK consumers. Some of those products will need FCA authorisation at launch, it warns, and others will grow into needing it later.

We’ve set out expectations for firms looking to develop and deploy personal AI agents in the financial services sector.

AI agents can widen access to financial tools and information, but can also blur the lines between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

#AI #FinancialRegulation #FinancialServices.

— Financial Conduct Authority (@TheFCA) November 24, 2026.

It has been revealed that the line gets crossed when an agent stops giving information and starts acting. Once it starts transactions, moves money, arranges borrowing, or makes investment calls, the firm behind it must work out which of those activities need approval.

The FCA has the power to step in where regulated services run without approval, and indicates it will use it if needed. The point, it says, is to guard against scams and make sure consumers get support and redress.

Tech companies get the bluntest passage. Describing a business as a technology provider does not remove the need for authorisation, the regulator claims. Parliament sets the boundary, not branding. It also notes a wrinkle of the AI era: the personalised context that large language models carry can make the legal questions harder, not easier.

Banks and other regulated firms keep full responsibility even when the AI comes from outside. Senior managers answer for the models in their area. The questions get very concrete: should a firm accept a payment ordered by an AI agent, or one from a digital wallet an agent controls?

There is help on offer too. The FCA’s AI Lab supports firms developing and testing agentic products. The regulator also aims an Agentic Policy Sprint for firms, policymakers, and tech providers. No date is set, but interest can be registered now.

The page lands as part of a coordinated push. Britain’s four digital regulators issued a joint statement on AI agents in October. On 16 November, they wrote to ministers, warning that several personal AI agents are about to launch in the UK and that some developers have yet to engage.

“We want to be explicit that existing legal and regulatory frameworks apply to personal AI agents,” the four regulators wrote in that statement.

In a recent development, on the back of the battery, there’s a window that showcases the liquid within the battery bank moving throughout it. This should help keep it a little bit cooler than most MagSafe battery banks.

I will admit, the battery bank is a little bit thick, and the lack of a kickstand is somewhat bothersome at this price point, especially when so many others offer one. That said, if heat is a concern of yours with MagSafe battery banks, this one will definitely solve that for you.

On the side, it offers a small display for showing battery percentage and charging speed.

One last thing of note: if you’re buying an iPhone Duo, this will stick out from the bottom of the phone. This is true for most MagSafe accessories on iPhone Duo, though.

It has been revealed that the UGREEN MagFlow battery bank comes in at $149, which is quite pricey for a MagSafe battery of any kind. For Black Friday, it’s on sale for just $90.23 on Amazon for Prime members, making it much more palatable if you’re looking for a MagSafe battery bank that doesn’t get as hot as the competition.

#165524. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5199 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Data centers already use light in networking.
  • The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” states Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The firm’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

Industry observers note that “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon claims this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the firm’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

According to recent reports, “The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” states Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen indicates, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

In a recent development, both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

Industry observers note that free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another major advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

It has been revealed that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” claims Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Industry observers note that in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Industry observers note that Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company unveiled a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

In a recent development, the energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main matter is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch notes, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” claims Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

It has been revealed that the Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

In a recent development, lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to rapidly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

LightSolver’s team is right now working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the manufacturer’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

In a recent development, yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick Newly introduced, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

Industry observers note that the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Latest claims. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Latest, Optalysis.

Industry observers note that instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

It has been revealed that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

It has been revealed that newly introduced says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

Sources indicate that how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he indicates. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. States Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” indicates Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print matter as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”.

The bigger question is: will the next MacBook Neo have a price increase? With additional RAM included, it feels inevitable.

Hopefully backlit keyboard if they increase price.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today, OpenAI released a blog post showing the perplexity of their models over time. The drop is impressive, and the claim is that perplexity itself can be a universal measure of intelligence.

After seeing this chart, the thought that came to mind was: perplexity against what? Perplexity is a measure of how well token likelihoods predict the actual next token. Perplexity is meaningless without knowing what text the model is trying to predict.

The answer was buried in a footnote. The chart is based on models predicting a fixed corpus of code.

Industry observers note that so the problem here is obvious. Could this chart just be a reflection of OpenAI models being increasingly trained on code?

In a recent development, I set about investigating this. My strategy was to find an open source repo with a tiny model and a documented training set, then monkey with it. While getting started, my agent found an existing paper that already did this. (The agent was Astra 6.2, funny enough. It must have low perplexity on this kind of tomfoolery.).

Industry observers note that the authors of the paper ran five training sets on a 160M model, varying only the proportion of the training data that was code. Here is what they found:.

Spoiler: the “internal model” here is the same 160M model with 75% of the training corpus being code.

As expected, if you look at perplexity on non-code text, it increases dramatically:.

Sources indicate that obviously, the model here with 75% code in the training corpus almost certainly is smarter at code. The point here isn’t that OpenAI’s chart measures nothing, only that their post should have a lot more qualifications [1].

[1] Funny enough, OpenAI does qualify in a single footnote about GPT-2 and GPT-3, saying “how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities.” Why they didn’t expand this to the rest of the models is anyone’s guess.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 23, 2026 at 8:15PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than eHealth ›.

It has been revealed that on its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, eHealth (EHTH -5.12%) announced that it remains on track for breakeven or better operating cash flow for the full year. For long-term shareholders, the health insurance marketplace is intentionally trimming low-margin sales volume to protect cash and build deeper member relationships. Three things management noted stand out.

Sources indicate that eHealth cut marketing spend during quiet seasonal periods to conserve capital while aiming for $90 million in total cost savings this year. Nine-month operating cash flow, the net cash generated by core operations, nearly doubled compared to the same period last year.

Recent findings suggest that insurance carriers are stabilizing after major benefit adjustments, leading them to restart marketing sponsorships with distribution partners. This turn benefits eHealth during the annual enrollment period (AEP), the autumn window when Medicare beneficiaries switch or select aims.

It might only be Tuesday, but the Black Friday deals have already arrived. And I've gotta say, I'm surprised at the headphone deals this year. I'm Pete, reviews editor here at Tom's Guide, and this is my fifth Black Friday working on the site. Normally, I have to concentrate to find legitimate deals through all the crappy ones — especially this early in the week.

In a recent development, this year, even well before the big day itself, I can't move for deals on many of the best headphones around. My favorite deals so far are on the Apple AirPods Max 2, which are reduced from $549 to $419 at Amazon; and the Sony WH-1000XM6, reduced from $459 to $348 at Amazon. But there are plenty more deals where those came from.

Soundcore's ever-faithful (and always cheap) Q20i have dropped in price early ahead of Black Friday. They're comfortable, lightweight headphones and sound great for the price, while also offering ANC — what more could you ask for under forty bucks?

In our Sony WH-CH530 review, we gave these plucky little cans a full five stars. Why? Because look at that $69 MSRP. That's why. For the money, these cans offer stellar sound, plenty of comfort, solid battery life and fun colorways! And now they're just $38.

"We heard you like bass, bro, so we put a bass slider in your headphones to make them literally shake on your head. There's a vibration motor in there. Seriously, bro, they're so bassy. And $110 off".

Industry observers note that sound, ANC, comfort, styling. These cans have it all. In fact, there was only one thing we didn't like in our Sony WH-CH730N review, and that was the U.S. price of $199 — way higher than the EU and U.K. relative pricing. Well, that's changed with this deal. For $99, the WH-CH730N are a hell of a lot of headphones for the money.

How about a very colorful pair of headphones for a great price? We're major fans of the fit, finish and sound of the JBL Live 780NC, and this Black Friday deal makes them a great bet if you've got a little more to spend (but still want to maximise those savings).

The venerable Beats Studio Pro hit different when they're $120 off MSRP. Solid ANC? Check. A cool, stylish look? Check. Good sound quality? That's a royal flush, baby.

In a recent development, bose might have replaced the QuietComfort headphones with (an also reduced pair), but at this price, these are headphones to go for. Excellent ANC for the price, a comfortable fit, and lovely physical controls. Not much more you could ask for.

Wanna look like Lobot, that pilot/butler dude from Cloud City in (the best) Star Wars? The Nothing Headphone (1) can help you live out that dream while offering solid customizable sound and a great control scheme. Not bad for a Black Friday deal.

According to recent reports, the Momentum 4 have a reputation of being a little... boring. If, that is, you consider some of the best-sounding headphones for the price and 60 hours of battery life boring. I don't — and neither does this massive $120 saving on the Sennheiser Momentum 4. They do look boring, though. I'll give you that.

The newly introduced cans have upgraded to the latest Bluetooth 6.0, a new removable (and therefore replaceable) battery, and some AI audio upscaling. Look, none of that was strictly necessary, as the XM4 were still fantastic anyway — even in 2026. But new features is never a bad thing.

Recent findings suggest that remember I stated up top that Bose made new headphones to replace its more affordable model? This be they, and they're $20 more than the ones that everyone is buying. If you want some snazzier colors and a new design, you've found the cans for you — the Bose QuietComfort Headphones 2nd gen.

Sonos's first attempt at headphones was a solid one, earning a coveted 4.5 stars in our Sonos Ace review. We loved the sound and noise cancelling, the battery life, the design and the integration with other Sonos gear. If you're an existing Sonos user, this is the deal for you.

Oh, look, boring raises its head again. If you consider 57 hours of battery life and excell... oh, I've made that joke before? Er... just buy the Momentum 4, not the Momentum 5. They're $160 and technically offer more battery life. Now that's no joke.

Sony's plastic fantastic weigh very little and sound excellent — and now you can get them for $100 off. Not that you should. You see, I'm something of a deals clairvoyant, and I can foresee a deeper discount in these headphones' future. I can also see you buying these anyway because you want to bag that low price. I don't blame you — the WH-1000XM6 are great after all.

Pure. Class. That's how I'd describe the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3. And I'd know, because I own and use a set of them on a near daily basis at home. The Px7 S3 have a warmer, bassier tune than the reference-tuned Px8 S2 (also on sale), but you still get that Bowers refinement and fidelity. Oh, and they're built like you'd expect from a luxury audio brand: bloomin' marvellously.

In a recent development, this isn't the lowest we've seen the AirPods Max 2 drop ($399)... but it's damn well close. And given these are the latest, greatest, and still rather upcoming'n'shiny flagships from Apple no less, $130 is a surprisingly good chunk of cash off.

Recent findings suggest that look, I'm a Bowers fanboy, I'll admit it. And I own the Px8 S2. So I have no problem giving some sage advice here: buy the Px8 S2, you won't regret it. Yes, they're pricey, but they make up for it with beautiful, spacious, high fidelity sound, exquisite build quality and strong ANC.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.
  • That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future ….
  • Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future ….

Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage occurred when two unrelated complications coincided. The next day saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication glitch affecting all air traffic control centers. A few days later, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Many Apple services went offline later the same week, with retail stores also affected. Finally, United Airlines had its own widespread IT outage that grounded a significant number of flights.

Each had their own unrelated causes, with the White House stating that rumors of an AI-facilitated systemic attack by a hostile state were false.

Sources indicate that however, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that we should expect future tech outages as a result of attacks facilitated by AI-discovered vulnerabilities. CNBC reports him issuing the warning on CNN’s State of the Union.

The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.

We already saw an example of this last month when a vulnerability discovered in PHP saw a significant number of websites being taken offline.

Microsoft President Brad Smith notes it isn’t just a question of bad actors exploiting vulnerabilities discovered by AI, but companies rushing to patch these may inadvertently cause systems to fail, as Newsweek reports.

What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you’re trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can’t take as much time to test what you’re changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong.

Major IT failures look set to be a routine event in the coming weeks and months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most dramatic shifts in the AI landscape is the emergence of intelligent agents that can use iPhone and Mac apps in order to carry out tasks on our behalf.

Sources indicate that we can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the organization even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start ….

The science fiction promise of AI has always been to be able to tell a computer what we want done and have the task carried out for us automatically. That’s starting to turn into a reality with the emergence of AI agents.

We’ve already seen Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Muse gain agent capabilities, and Apple is expected to bring these to Siri AI at some point next year.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that the company ultimately wants to go in this direction and may add these abilities next year. CEO John Ternus has reportedly been pushing Craig Federighi for faster software development, with specific mention of “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” which seems likely to mean agentic capabilities.

Last week also saw a since-deleted Apple job listing detailing intends for autonomous AI agents.

According to recent reports, we’ve already seen some of the ways in which this can go wrong, and we recently outlined three significant risks. Wired reports that banks are now responding to these by either blocking AI agents or warning customers that using them can be dangerous.

Wells Fargo even goes as far as using capitals in its latest terms, stating that it will not be responsible for the consequences.

Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK.

We can likely expect similar pushback in sectors like online shopping as companies fear high returns costs and other consequences from mistakes by AI agents.

Personally, I don’t give any AI agents access to any of my banking or other financial services, considering the risks to be too high. I don’t see my position changing any time soon.

What’s your take? Would you trust an AI agent with access to your bank accounts? If not, would Apple launching agentic capabilities for Siri AI change your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

  • By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 23, 2026 at 8:36PM EST.
  • On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov.
  • Assurant's Connected Living segment, which provides protection prepares for mobile phones and consumer electronics, expanded as customers kept devices longer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 23, 2026 at 8:36PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Assurant ›.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Assurant (AIZ +0.76%) raised its full-year earnings outlook following double-digit profit growth across its primary operating units. Long-term investors benefit when high-margin protection programs scale through multiyear partnerships. These programs generate predictable cash flows that fund ongoing share repurchases. Three key takeaways from management's presentation highlight the forces driving this business forward.

Assurant's Connected Living segment, which provides protection prepares for mobile phones and consumer electronics, expanded as customers kept devices longer. The firm processed 22 million devices annually through its reverse logistics business, which manages returns and trade-ins for mobile carriers. High device counts keep unit costs low and widen the company's cost advantage over smaller rivals.

In a recent development, in its Global Housing segment, Assurant relies heavily on lender-placed insurance, which provides mandatory property coverage when a homeowner's policy lapses. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • It remarked that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so ….
  • Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nvidia has revealed that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The organization’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It remarked that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so ….

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The Latest York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

Money over country. This is government intervention.

Despite putting the tech giant at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, stated that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones said: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”.

That changed today, with the company making the announcement in a press release.

Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

According to recent reports, “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” noted Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a fresh industrial revolution,” noted Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”.

As previously declared, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
