Just a Few Bugs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Justafewbugs

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I'm an independent security researcher.
  • Industry observers note that for most of the past year I've been working on Google's current Pixel phones.
  • In total, the VRP has paid me $250, in a single payment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'm an independent security researcher. Over the years I've reported vulnerabilities to a number of vendors and manufacturers, and several of those reports have become CVEs.

Industry observers note that for most of the past year I've been working on Google's current Pixel phones. I reverse engineered the Samsung radio stack (under embargo), the IMS and RTP media code, the Trusty trusted apps, the MediaTek M90 modem RIL and the Android telephony framework, amongst other things. In that time I filed 95 reports through the Android and Google Devices Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP), and around 95% of them came with a working proof of concept.

In total, the VRP has paid me $250, in a single payment.

I should say at the outset that I have nothing against Google. My project Box began as a fork of their AI Edge Gallery; I've worked on it most days for a year, and Google have taken features from my fork back into their own. I also maintain Iris, a hardened fork of Chromium. Much of what I do is built on Google's work. This page is solely about what happened to the security bugs I reported through their programme over twelve months.

In a recent development, bugs were fixed after being closed. For every closed report, I extracted the relevant binary from Google's current factory image and compared the exact function the report referred to. Eight had been fixed in shipped code, with a bounds check, a permission or a validation step added precisely where I'd noted one was missing. All eight had originally been closed as a "duplicate" or as "not a vulnerability". None was paid and none was credited. Two more have since been fixed in the QPR3 beta.

Bugs were closed for reasons the code doesn't bear out. More than a dozen others were closed as duplicate, infeasible or "can't reproduce", yet the defect is still there, unchanged, in the current build. I'm not suggesting anyone owes a reward for a bug that hasn't been fixed, and I'm not claiming one. My point is simply that the stated reasons for closing them don't hold up once you look at the binary.

A reward promised in writing has never been paid. In January Google confirmed a valid bug and raised both its severity and its reward, in writing. Three months later they reversed all of it, with no new evidence. They then mentioned they would "stand by our word" and pay $250 anyway as a "discretionary payment exception". That was in January. Ten months of "processing", "soon" and "no date" later, it still hasn't been paid. The report itself was submitted before December 2025.

One line in that thread still puzzles me. Google told me in writing that they were paying the Safety Center reward "even though our final technical assessment rated it as a duplicate of a report with no security impact." If the bug had no security impact, there is nothing to pay for. If it's worth paying for, then it did have an impact. Both statements are in the same ticket.

Everything in the tables below is a closed report, and Google's wording is quoted directly from the issue tracker. I've deliberately left out the technical details of the three reports that are still "Assigned", along with anything under active coordinated disclosure.

Every report on this page is a closed ticket. Google's own position, stated on these tickets, is that they do not grant or deny permission for disclosure and that researchers are free to publish at their discretion. Nothing still under assessment or active coordinated disclosure is included here.

I followed the same process for every closed report in the tables:.

Each report was given one of four verdicts: PATCHED (a check has been added that wasn't there when I reported it), STILL PRESENT (the code is unchanged), N/A (reported against this exact build, or Google described it as intended design) and CANT-DETERMINE (the binary is missing or the build doesn't match).

I didn't rely on Google's security bulletins or the supplementary patch lists. A silent fix with no bulletin entry and no credit won't appear there by definition, so the only way to find one is to compare the shipped code yourself.

Sources indicate that this concerns ticket 467575499 / 470814942. On 23 January 2026 Google wrote that they had "confirmed this is a valid bug", were "increasing severity" and "increasing reward", and would "matter a payment for the fresh amount once it has been processed". On 24 April, without any further analysis, they reversed all three. In what they called a "Final Assessment", the same bug now "does not qualify for a reward or severity increase".

Sources indicate that in June they wrote that they wished to "stand by our word regarding the reward". On 10 July they set out the figures: "$250 for Safety Center, $250 for the mic bug, $500USD total". They described this as "honoring our initial promise", whilst still referring to the Safety Center half as a duplicate with no security impact. The microphone half was paid. The Safety Center half was moved into a "discretionary payment exception" with, in their words, no "exact credit date". The most recent reply, in October, notes much the same: still approved, still no date.

Not every report ended as a duplicate or "not a vulnerability". In this case Google's own panel rated the report High severity, High quality and assigned it for remediation. The fix has since shipped three times: in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) in October, in the public November stable build (CP4A.261105.040.D1), and in the latest QPR3 beta (DP11.261030.003). The ticket is still marked "Assigned", and the reward and CVE fields are still blank, so I've kept the vulnerability itself out of this write-up. The screenshots below show only the process: a report Google rated High and confirmed in writing as eligible for a reward, then left sitting at "Assigned" after the very condition they had set had been met.

It isn't the only one. A second, unrelated report was also rated High severity, High quality by the same panel. A month later it is still "Assigned", the reward is still "with the panel" and the ASR fields are still blank. I haven't named the report or included any technical detail; the screenshots show only the rating and the state of the reward.

According to recent reports, when Google closes a report as a duplicate, it's closed against an internal "canonical" bug ID. I asked for the IDs behind several of mine. For two entirely unrelated bugs they gave me the same internal ID, 479203197: one was a Rust keystore panic in a trusted app, the other a C++ out-of-bounds read in the RTP media parser. They're written in different languages, sit in different subsystems and belong to different teams. A single internal report cannot be the original for both.

Google acknowledged this in writing on both tickets: "Giving you this ID for your other report was a mistake on our end," and, separately, "we made a mistake when linking the duplicate tickets." So at least one supposedly verified duplicate was marked as such without anyone checking it against the report it named.

Sources indicate that many of my reports followed the same course. Filed, assigned, worked on by an engineer, and then, months later and with no fresh technical comment in between, quietly changed to Duplicate. The original is always an internal ticket I can't view, usually accompanied by a note that it was "previously reported by an internal Google engineer". I have no means of seeing that report, confirming that it exists, or confirming that it predates mine.

There are a great many of these. Of the 95 reports I've filed, 34 were closed as duplicates. A few of those are my own resubmissions and appeals folded back together, so it comes to roughly 26 distinct findings that Google accepted as real and then attributed to a report I'm not allowed to see. A duplicate isn't a rejection: it's Google confirming that the bug exists and saying someone else found it first. In 26 of my cases, that someone was an internal engineer who, by Google's account, found the identical bug in the same month I did, in firmware that had only just been released.

It's the timing I keep coming back to. I always work from the current month's factory image, so every report I file concerns firmware released that month, often only a few days earlier. When a bug I found in an image that shipped last week comes back weeks later as something Google has apparently had open internally for months, I'm in no position to check it, and it happens again and again.

According to recent reports, on the one occasion I pressed hard enough to find out which build the original was filed against, the explanation was at least plausible. Report 549662989 was marked as a duplicate of one filed against a Pixel 10 (blazer:16/CP1A.260505.005), and PixelModemService ships the same code on both generations, so I accepted it. That was the exception. The ID mix-up described above indicates what the process looks like when I can actually check it: the same internal ID given as the "original" for two completely unrelated bugs, and admitted in writing to be a mistake. If one supposedly verified duplicate was marked without anyone comparing it to the report it named, I've no reason to assume the two dozen I can't check were handled any more carefully.

The DCMO DcmoReceiver bug is a case in point. Google say my re-filed report (585012607) duplicates 545652324, which they describe as having been filed on 12 August 2026 by another external researcher, with the same root cause. I can't confirm any of that. Opening 545652324 returns "Access denied", as has every other original I've been referred to, so the date, the author and the root cause are Google's word alone. What I can check is the code, and the defect is still present and unpatched in CP4A.261105.040.D1, months after the date they give for the original report.

Early on, Google closed one of my findings with their standard message: "not a security vulnerability, logged for potential remediation in a future version, considered closed". They later withdrew it in writing: "You are completely correct. This finding is indeed a legitimate security vulnerability. It was incorrectly closed as 'not a security vulnerability' due to an oversight during triage of this specific ticket.".

Recent findings suggest that the same template has since been used to close several more of my reports. On my own tickets alone it has been shown to be wrong more than once, by Google's own admission, and the glitch was subsequently patched using the code I had submitted.

Industry observers note that from now on, whenever Google closes one of my reports, I'll publish it here. The two reports below were closed in the same way, so it's worth being precise about what happened. Both had already been assigned and triaged. A Google triager then manually moved each one back to "New", and a minute later, from the same personal account, posted a message describing itself as "an automatically generated message" from the "Google Security Bot". The message closed the report as Won't Fix (Intended Behavior) on the grounds of a rate limit, and stated "we will not be able to see any of your responses".

Recent findings suggest that the genuinely automated messages on my tickets come from a separate system account. These came from the person who had handled the ticket manually a minute before, which is difficult to reconcile with an automated rate limiter. The second report was closed in this way even after I'd supplied a full reproduction on a locked, release-keys phone. Both defects can be verified directly from the shipping image.

This is ticket 559521028. The MediaTek RIL on the Pixel 11 (libmtkmipc-ril.so, loaded by mtkfusionrild) reimplements the AOSP SMS, WAP push and 3GPP2 parsers in native C++, but keeps AOSP's habit of indexing buf[i] without checking bounds. In Java, reading past the end of a buffer throws an exception that gets caught. In native code nothing is thrown, so an over-read leaks memory and an over-write corrupts it.

According to recent reports, there are two defects. Both can be reached with a single incoming SMS, with no user interaction and no app installed:.

In a recent development, use the leak to defeat ASLR, then use the write to corrupt a chosen object. That's the standard route to remote code execution in rild, the radio daemon, which runs as the radio user and has a direct channel to the baseband.

I was particularly specific about how the code is reached. The RIL does have one sanity check on PDUs, smsDeliverPduCheck, but it only sits on the branch that forwards the raw PDU to the framework. The native parser is reached by a separate path, from dispatchSms to onHandleSmsMessage to dispatchSuplMsg to SmsMessage::createFromPdu, with no check on it at all. That path depends on a SUPL gate, doesSuplExist(), which returns true for as long as rild is running on any normal device: its global is initialised to 2 in .data (confirmed in the shipped binary) and changes to 1 as soon as MediaTek's location daemon starts. The unchecked parser therefore runs on every incoming SMS, and the trigger can be a silent Type 0 SMS that the user never sees.

In a recent development, I re-checked both defects in three shipped builds: the October stable release (CD1A.261005.003), the November stable release (CP4A.261105.040.D1, SPL 2026-11-05) and the DP11 QPR3 beta. No bounds check had been added to any of these paths.

According to recent reports, this is static analysis of the shipped binary. I don't have a modem test rig, as the report makes clear, so there's no runtime exploit attached. On 12 November the team asked for a live software proof of concept. Two days later, on 14 November, the report was closed as Won't Fix (Infeasible) with the template "we have investigated this issue and determined that this is not a security vulnerability... logged for potential remediation in a future version", and the ASR Severity field was set to NSBC. That is the same template Google have already withdrawn on another of my reports, here applied to an unchecked, attacker-controlled memcpy length in the radio daemon that can be reached with zero clicks and is still present in the shipping build.

It has been revealed that A few more of the closed reports, kept short. Each is the bug, roughly how it works, and how it is reached.

Sources indicate that an OTA enhancement the device will install, signed by the wrong key (ticket 541986810, closed Duplicate). RecoverySystem.verifyPackage is the check that decides whether an update package is really signed by Google. It looks at two certificates and never confirms they are the same one. The trust check looks at the certificate sitting first in the package. The signature is then verified against a different certificate, chosen by an issuer and serial number that are also read from the package. So an attacker puts Google's genuine, public signing certificate first to pass the trust check, puts their own certificate further in, points the signature at that one, and signs the package with their own key. The check passes for a package they signed. It is reached through the sideload or update path, where the signature gate that is supposed to stop an unofficial package does not.

DNS still leaves the phone when you turn on "Block connections without VPN" (ticket 552188030, closed Duplicate). VPN lockdown is meant to stop any traffic that is not inside the tunnel. DNS queries are left exempt from that block, for every app, not just the device's own traffic. So even with lockdown on, an app's DNS lookups leave the device outside the VPN, which leaks which sites are being resolved and gives a channel the lockdown is supposed to close.

Recent findings suggest that any app can switch off your Lock-on-Disconnect (ticket 552305734, closed Infeasible, still present). The Cross-Device stack exports a broadcast receiver, PermissionBroadcastReceiver, with no permission on it, and it acts on the broadcast without checking who sent it. Any installed app, holding no permissions, can send that broadcast and force an immediate un-enrollment of the user's Lock-on-Disconnect security feature, turning off a protection the user had switched on.

In a recent development, the share sheet fetching a picture it should not (ticket 538314136, closed Infeasible, still present). The intent resolver renders a caller-supplied icon URI without checking the caller is allowed to read it. An app hands it a URI that points at content belonging to another user or profile, and a privileged process fetches it on the attacker's behalf and hands it back.

According to recent reports, any app cancelling another app's on-device AI model load (ticket 558472707, closed Infeasible, still present). cancelModelLoad in the NPU manager service does not check who is calling, so any app can cancel a different app's model load and deny it the hardware AI path.

A radio service you can crash with one value (ticket 555984702, closed Can't Reproduce, still present). The grilservice radio-config path reads an array size straight from an incoming parcel with no cap and allocates it. A crafted size forces a huge allocation and takes the service down, dropping telephony.

It has been revealed that any app can bind the Play Store's setup service (ticket 564059393, closed Working As Intended). Play Store exports IPlaySetupServiceV2, and the permission meant to guard it declares no protection level, so Android treats it as a normal permission and auto-grants it to any app that asks. Any installed app can then bind the service. The same pattern, a guard permission with no protection level so it auto-grants, turned up across 31 exported components in the shipped image.

Recent findings suggest that an unprotected "setup finished" broadcast that rewrites your system locale (ticket 563958561, closed Infeasible). SETUP_WIZARD_FINISHED is not a protected broadcast, so any app can send it. Nine privileged, system-UID receivers act on it, and one of them persistently rewrites the device's system locale. A zero-permission app sends one broadcast and changes a system-wide setting it has no right to touch.

According to recent reports, A preinstalled app slipping past the account-ownership check (ticket 559524832, closed Infeasible). AccountManagerService.isSystemUid() actually tests whether the caller is preinstalled, not whether it is the system UID. Any preinstalled app therefore passes a guard meant only for the system, and can see and remove accounts it does not own.

Recent findings suggest that faking that you are standing next to your car (ticket 560453159, closed Can't Reproduce). Two chained UWB bugs: one leaks the secure-ranging session key, the other hijacks the Digital Key radio path. Together a zero-permission app could spoof the physical proximity that passive car entry relies on, without being anywhere near the vehicle.

One Wi-Fi frame reading out of bounds in the kernel (ticket 568933934, closed Can't Reproduce). An unsigned integer underflow in the Broadcom Wi-Fi driver's QoS-Map action-frame handler causes an out-of-bounds read in kernel heap memory. A single 25-byte 802.11 action frame from a nearby Wi-Fi peer triggers it, with no association or pairing.

In a recent development, A VoLTE call message that hangs the IMS stack (ticket 560878423, closed Can't Reproduce). A SIP message with a negative Content-Length is parsed as a signed value, the offset goes negative, and the receive loop never ends. One zero-click message puts the VoLTE/IMS stack into a permanent hang.

Any app reading and tampering with your Now Playing history (ticket 562215877, closed Infeasible). Private Compute Services exports NowPlayingRelayService as a binder with no caller check, unlike four sibling services in the same app. Any installed app can read and alter the record of music the phone has recognised around you.

Any app triggering a recognition pass and reading the result (ticket 561838690, closed Infeasible). The Android System Intelligence MusicRelayService binder does no caller check across its 19 transactions, so any app can read your Now Playing history and silently start a latest recognition pass, listening to what is around you.

It has been revealed that an RCS suggestion that runs JavaScript in-app with one tap (ticket 572199671, closed Working As Intended). Google Messages' blocklist for RCS suggested-action URLs misses the javascript: and data: schemes, so a crafted suggestion loads into a JavaScript-enabled bridged WebView, and one tap runs the attacker's JavaScript inside the app.

Industry observers note that any app reading the CBRS radio database and its coordinates (ticket 579289116, closed Duplicate). The CbsdContentProvider in SCONE is exported with no guard, so any installed app can read the CBRS CBSD database, including the CBSD location coordinates, that it should have no access to.

Recent findings suggest that A Wi-Fi attribute reading out of bounds in the kernel (ticket 547477982, closed Duplicate). The Broadcom Wi-Fi driver does not validate a NAN SDEA attribute length before using it, so a crafted value causes an out-of-bounds read in kernel memory. It is reachable from a nearby Wi-Fi peer.

A system service handed the keys to start anything (ticket 558470054, closed Infeasible). dcservice, an app-tier component, is given the SELinux permission to start any init service, the only domain on the whole device with that broad grant, and for a capability its own code never uses. It is exactly the kind of over-grant that turns a small foothold into a larger one.

The SDK sandbox taking attacker file paths (ticket 561840524, closed Can't Reproduce). computeSdkStorage is the one method on the SDK Runtime sandbox service that is missing the check that the caller is the system server, so any zero-permission app can bind the service and call it with paths of its choosing.

A two-byte location message that exhausts the stack (ticket 568936058, closed Can't Reproduce). The GNSS daemon's SUPL message framing recurses into itself with no base case when a message declares a zero length, so a two-byte message drives it into infinite recursion and crashes the daemon.

A WAP-push SMS that quietly kills texting (ticket 543183960, closed Infeasible). A malformed WAP-push message lands in a loop with an empty catch block, so instead of failing cleanly the telephony process hangs and SMS silently stops working.

It has been revealed that A SIP message body that overflows a stack buffer (ticket 540746953, closed Duplicate). The IMS SIP encoder copies a message body into a fixed 65535-byte array on the stack with no cap, so an oversized body overflows it.

Recent findings suggest that an eUICC upgrade any app can kick off (ticket 532021672, closed Infeasible). StartOtaReceiver is exported and unprotected, so any unprivileged app can trigger the eUICC OTA flow by sending the broadcast it listens for.

A system app that fetches URLs for you (ticket 537921665, closed Working As Intended). ConfigUpdater's exported receivers take a URL from broadcast extras and fetch it, with no checks, so an app with no INTERNET permission can make a system app perform requests on its behalf, a server-side request forgery.

Industry observers note that tethered traffic walking straight past VPN lockdown (ticket 552196751, closed Infeasible). "Block connections without VPN" does not cover tethered clients, so anything connected over USB, Ethernet or the Wi-Fi hotspot bypasses the VPN entirely. Google closed it as working by construction.

Any app repainting the real enterprise-enrollment screen (ticket 552200665, closed Infeasible). A zero-permission app can drive the phone's genuine enterprise-enrollment screen and place its own logo on it, on demand, which is the groundwork for a convincing enrollment phish.

In a recent development, impersonating another process by renaming yourself (ticket 559533853, closed Infeasible). The process-monitor daemon identifies the process it watches only by reading /proc/pid/cmdline, with no UID check when the vendor config leaves the uid out. Any app can set its own process name to match the target and be treated as it.

An NFC firmware-update reply read past its buffer (ticket 537923579, closed Duplicate). The NFC firmware-update handler indexes into the response from the NFC chip using a length it does not check. It sits on the trust boundary with the physically attached NFC controller.

Recent findings suggest that any app making a system installer install an APK (ticket 563677600, closed Duplicate). WebAppService runs as a privileged app holding INSTALL_PACKAGES. By declaring a single intent-filter, any zero-permission app can make it install an APK, borrowing its install privilege.

In a recent development, A CDMA text message that overflows the radio daemon's stack (ticket 568929629, closed Duplicate). The MediaTek RIL's CDMA CT-WAP SMS decoder (BearerData::specialProcessForCtWapPush) writes past a fixed buffer on a crafted message, with no interaction. This is the write half of the SMS chain described above, filed on its own.

Industry observers note that A reported heap write in the Messages image decoder (ticket 537918512, closed Working As Intended). A crafted animated-WebP image delivered by MMS or RCS, where the frame-disposal step in libframesequence was reported to clear a region using a width and height taken from the file without clamping them, overflowing the pixel buffer. Google closed it Working As Intended, and unlike most of the entries here I could not fully confirm the path in the shipped binary, so it is listed as reported and closed rather than verified.

Each row is a closed report, checked against Google's current factory image. "Fixed" means the code the report described has changed: the report was right, the fix shipped, the ticket stayed closed and nothing was paid.

Recent findings suggest that that's eight tickets, closed as duplicate or infeasible, that have been fixed in the shipping image. I re-checked all eight against the October builds and the fixes are still in place.

Two more have been fixed in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) but not yet in a stable release:.

It has been revealed that on 30 October 2026 another researcher independently disclosed a zero-click WAP push crash in Android's telephony stack (smsofdeath.com), which has been reported here: cybersecuritynews.com/zero-click-android-vulnerability. A single malformed WAP push SMS causes WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu to allocate an array from an unvalidated, truncated header length. This throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException that kills the telephony process, and because the carrier keeps redelivering the unacknowledged message, one SMS becomes a recurring outage.

I reported that exact defect twice, with the root cause in WspTypeDecoder and WapPushOverSms traced frame by frame, and a working proof against the shipped decoder:.

Both were closed as duplicates of internal report 517376969, which Google say was filed by their internal automated testing in late May 2026. The fix, a bounds check before the allocation, shipped in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) and is still missing from the current stable build. On 30 October 2026 Google told me on the record that, because their internal tool found it first, my reports are "not eligible for a reward".

So in this one pair of tickets you can see the whole pattern: reported early, verified against the source, closed as a duplicate, fixed without comment in a later build, disclosed publicly by someone else, and never paid.

Industry observers note that the clearest way to see this is to put two factory images with the same patch level side by side. Take the WAP push crash (538367541 / 543174762, closed as Duplicate) and the SIM Toolkit crash (555981160, closed as "not reproducible" and later changed to Duplicate). Both are closed, and neither was paid.

The same file, at the same security patch level, in two builds:.

The bug was real enough to fix, and the fix is in a shipping build. Yet the report that found it, and described that exact fix, was closed as a duplicate or a non-issue and paid nothing. The credit went instead to an internal report I'm not allowed to see, filed on a date I can't verify, against firmware that had only just been released.

In a recent development, I'm not claiming payment for any of these; none of them has been fixed. They're listed because the reason given for closing each one doesn't match the code. The defect is still there, unchanged, in the current factory image. Every one of these reports has been closed.

In a recent development, other researchers have described much the same experience with Google's reward programmes. These are the cases that have been reported publicly.

Sources indicate that config Connector, 2026. In June 2026 The Register reported on Justin O'Leary's "ConfigConfusion" flaw in Google Config Connector, which allowed a user in one Kubernetes namespace to obtain organisation owner rights in GCP. He reported it on 8 March. Google replied "Nice catch!", rated it P1/S1 and accepted it, then reversed its position, said the product was working as intended and refused the reward. Google's view was that not paying a reward "does not mean that the product team won't fix the concern". Months later the ticket still highlighted as accepted, with no CVE and no fix. O'Leary's argument was straightforward: if it needs fixing, it isn't intended behaviour, and if it isn't intended behaviour, it qualifies for a reward.

Antigravity, 2025. When Google rolled out its Antigravity AI coding tool, researchers at Mindgard reported that a tampered workspace could plant code that would run every time the application started. Google closed the report on 21 November as "Won't Fix (Intended Behavior)", and only reopened and escalated it after Mindgard published their findings four days later. The issue was later fixed.

Pixel lock screen bypass, 2022. David Schütz found that he could unlock a Pixel without its passcode by swapping the SIM card and entering the PUK code. He reported it in June 2022 and, some months later, was told it was a duplicate. The earlier report was one Google had been unable to reproduce. Only after he kept pressing, and demonstrated the bypass to Google engineers in person, was it fixed in the November 2022 update (CVE-2022-20465). He was paid $70,000, rather than the $100,000 available for a lock screen bypass, because his report was still treated as a duplicate.

In 2020 CSO Online covered the wider problem (J.M. Porup, "Bug bounty platforms buy researcher silence, violate labor laws, critics say"). Critics in that piece, including legal scholars such as Amit Elazari and Katie Moussouris, argue that these programmes can be used to suppress disclosure, that researchers often have no legal safe harbour, and that the model raises questions under labour law. The description of researchers as disposable contractors whose finished work can be rejected without recourse is mine, not theirs.

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Sources indicate that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • Industry observers note that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Sources indicate that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon declared his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Sources indicate that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

Industry observers note that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash newly introduced competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

According to recent reports, amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is crucial because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

Recent findings suggest that I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

Recent findings suggest that RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company unveiled a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

In a recent development, but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s key to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Industry observers note that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s presently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

In a recent development, but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

According to recent reports, A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Sources indicate that last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky promptly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a fresh instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

It has been revealed that in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

According to recent reports, though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the tech giant’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Industry observers note that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Recent findings suggest that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Recent findings suggest that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its consumers because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted looks for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

In a recent development, even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the firm judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

In a recent development, this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

#165504. Modernizing iperf/iperf3 and introducing fireperf

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (668 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Daniel-baumann ↗ Open Full Page

Modernizing iperf/iperf3 and introducing fireperf

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Daniel-baumann

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently I spend some time on modernizing the packaging of the Internet Protocol bandwidth measuring tools iperf and iperf3 in Debian, as well as uploading fireperf to Debian.
  • Sources indicate that previously, src:iperf only built iperf.
  • Apart from tidying the Debian package, src:iperf now builds the new iperf-client and iperf-server packages, the latter contains the systemd and ufw integration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently I spend some time on modernizing the packaging of the Internet Protocol bandwidth measuring tools iperf and iperf3 in Debian, as well as uploading fireperf to Debian.

Sources indicate that previously, src:iperf only built iperf. If you wanted to run an iperf server, you had to do it on your own, i.e. there was no systemd service for that.

Apart from tidying the Debian package, src:iperf now builds the new iperf-client and iperf-server packages, the latter contains the systemd and ufw integration. iperf-server runs with a dynamic systemd user and systemd service hardening.

It has been revealed that the iperf package is now a transitional package, that also cleans up any leftovers from before the package split into iperf-client and iperf-server (e.g. when upgrading from trixie to forky).

For historical reasons, iperf2 is packaged in debian as iperf, not iperf2. Now the iperf packages have provides for iperf2, iperf2-client, and iperf2-server respectively (so they can be installed by these names too).

Updated iperf packages are available in sid, and backports for trixie are available at Debian Fast Forward.

It might make sense in the future….

given that iperf2 and iperf3 are completely different tools with different advantages and disadvantages depending on the use-case.

therefore the one is not replacing the other (iperf2 in general is the better tool than iperf3, eventhough the common misconception is that iperf3 is supposedly better than iperf2 because the number 3 is greater than the number 2).

…to maybe rename iperf to iperf2 to match both upstream naming and also to harmonize the packaging of iperf2 with other distributions.

Previously, src:iperf3 only built iperf3. If you wanted to run an iperf3 server, iperf3 had a debconf yes/no question which would then start one iperf3 server on the default port 5201.

Apart from tidying the Debian package, src:iperf3 now builds the new iperf3-client and iperf3-server packages, the latter contains the systemd and ufw integration. iperf3-server runs with a dynamic systemd user instead of the previous local system account, and has systemd service hardening.

Since iperf3 (contrary to iperf, also see here and here for iperv vs. iperf3) does not allow using multiple connections on the same port, you have to run multiple iperf3 servers, each on their own port, in order to serve more than one client at the time.

The old debconf question for enabling a single iperf3 server has been removed as well as the obsolete sysvinit integration.

In order to allow running multiple iperf3 servers at the same time (but on different ports), iperf3-server now contains a systemd service template so you can enable multiple iperf3 servers (e.g. 3 servers on subsequent port numbers, but you can run as many as you want on any ports you like) either manually with:.

or by using debconf interactively to do it automatically for you (which defaults to one instance on port 5201):.

or by using debconf non-interactively to do it automatically for you:.

The iperf3 package is now a transitional package, that also cleans up any leftovers from before the package split into iperf3-client and iperf3-server.

Updated iperf3 packages are available in sid, and backports for trixie are available at Debian Fast Forward.

Image 1: fireperf interactive terminal interface.

Image 2: fireperf non-interactive terminal interface.

fireperf is a modern take on the iperf3 network performance and stress-testing tool under the IPFire project umbrella:.

measures upload or download individually, or concurrent upload and download.

allows to serve many clients in parallel (on the same port).

allows to use many workers in parallel (for maxing out bandwith of servers with LACP instead of ECMP).

allows to use and track many connection sessions in parallel (for maxing out firewalls).

can also be used as a client for both iperf and iperf3 (autodetecting the target).

can also be used as a iperf3 server.

uses less CPU ressources on both the client and the server (io_uring, zerocopy, …).

fireperf packages are in sid, and backports for trixie are available at Debian Fast Forward.

#165502. Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials.
  • All of this could potentially be put at risk by the organization’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….
  • In a recent development, apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the organization’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….

In a recent development, apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The tech giant has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the manufacturer hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I noted at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the tech giant’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

Recent findings suggest that after its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the firm set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple noted it was 95% of the way there.

Sources indicate that the organization also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and Latest Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

Potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai mentioned that the AI boom was “challenging” to the company’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the organization is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”.

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

In a recent development, at the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the manufacturer’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report stated the tech giant had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

However, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

It has been revealed that what happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the organization moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li claims. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the tech giant will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”.

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the tech giant’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Rick Orford – Nov 23, 2026 at 8:38PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Blackstone ›.

BlackRock (BLK +3.88%) and Blackstone (BX +4.57%) each oversee more than $1 trillion in assets, making them two of the largest asset management firms worldwide. But with one trading closer to its 52-week high and the other down sharply this year, the question is: Which stock offers the more attractive opportunity for buyers?

BlackRock offers exposure to one of the most diversified businesses in asset management. With $15.5 trillion in assets under management (AUM) at the end of the third quarter, up 15% from the previous year, the organization has built an enormous platform spanning index funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and private markets.

On top of that, the company sees broad demand, attracting massive inflows across equities, fixed-income investments, alternative investments, and cash. For example, its iShares ETF business remains an important growth engine, while its active investment strategies attract capital from investors seeking opportunities beyond passive index investing.

Its third-quarter performance further strengthened the bull case in favor of the stock. Its third-quarter revenue rose 19% year over year, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 38%. Looking ahead, its ability to attract latest money while expanding its technology and private markets businesses gives it several avenues for continued earnings growth.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/23/26.

The main drawback is valuation. So far this year, BlackRock stock is up about 5% and trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio based on estimated earnings performance of about 18, which means investors are paying about $18 for every $1 of expected earnings. That leaves less room for error if market conditions deteriorate or inflows slow down.

Another manufacturer has also built its business around alternative assets, giving investors exposure to private equity, real estate, and infrastructure.

Blackstone has also established itself as one of the biggest names in alternative-asset management, with $1.4 trillion in AUM as of the third quarter. More broadly, its latest results suggest that investor demand remains healthy despite a challenging backdrop for private markets. Specifically, the company attracted $63.3 billion in fresh money, bringing its trailing 12-month (TTM) inflows to $271.6 billion.

It has been revealed that beyond inflows, one encouraging development is the growth of its perpetual capital business, which reached $562 billion. These investment vehicles are designed to provide capital without the fixed fund life and fundraising cycles associated with traditional private equity funds. This gives Blackstone a larger pool of relatively stable capital that can support more predictable fee revenue over time.

Industry observers note that blackstone is also benefiting from several major investment themes, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), energy infrastructure, and private credit. After all, building data centers, expanding electricity capacity, and financing AI infrastructure requires enormous amounts of capital. And Blackstone has established investment platforms across all these themes, allowing it to participate in the biggest opportunities of the next decade.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/23/26.

It has been revealed that blackstone shares have fallen almost 27% this year, but that has made its valuation more reasonable, with the stock trading at a forward P/E of about 16. Looking ahead, if transaction activity improves and fundraising accelerates, the stock could recover well.

Overall, both BlackRock and Blackstone offer exposure to the growing asset management industry, but their valuations and growth drivers present different opportunities for investors.

According to recent reports, blackRock offers scale, diversification, and strong earnings growth, making it appealing to investors seeking steady long-term growth, although its premium valuation limits the margin for error. Blackstone offers exposure to private markets and AI infrastructure at a considerably lower price, potentially giving investors greater upside if the manufacturer recovers. In other words, these giants appeal to different buyers: BlackRock is steadier, Blackstone is riskier. But each looks like a buy.

iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017.
  • Recent findings suggest that with iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch.
  • According to recent reports, the setup is simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

Recent findings suggest that with iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the latest GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

According to recent reports, the setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

Industry observers note that as a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

According to recent reports, gymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

In a recent development, airPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

In a recent development, iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods customers a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

In testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t revision as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk showed 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

According to recent reports, I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

Recent findings suggest that does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

Industry observers note that what is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

Industry observers note that if I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

It has been revealed that airPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.
