Apple Music adds a pair of upgrades in iOS 27.3. Selfie Sing is an all-fresh feature that lets you record short videos of yourself singing along to your favorite songs, aided by onscreen lyrics. It’s perfect for sharing on TikTok or other social platforms.

It has been revealed that if you’re not the type to share karaoke videos online, another nice iOS 27.3 change is that the lyrics view for songs has gotten an iPhone Duo-inspired upgrade in landscape mode. Now, artwork for the song you’re listening to blends beautifully into the stream of lyrics.

Apple’s Health app gets a major overhaul in iOS 27.3, though only for Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhones.

The new Health app has an Insights tab for personalized data visualization and guidance, Longevity tab for tracking your health age, and there are new features like educational videos, movement evaluations, and the ability to order labs that get automatically imported into the app.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here.

Vertical video is coming with a latest Clips feature that lets you browse short samples of Apple TV shows and movies in a TikTok-style vertically scrolling format.

Video podcasts are also coming to the TV app, with the option to automatically sync playback from Apple Podcasts inside the TV app.

Apple Fitness+ is getting a big expansion in iOS 27.3 with a fresh Gym Strength program.

Gym Strength lets you build a strength program that fits your schedule and the equipment you have on hand. It’s fully customizable and provides Apple’s best offering yet for traditional strength training.

Whether you’re brand latest to strength training or just benefit from some additional structure, Gym Strength is a great reason to try out Fitness+.

Industry observers note that apple’s Freeform app gets a handful of improvements in iOS 27.3, including new text styling options and preset background colors to choose from. You can also generate custom shapes using Apple Intelligence.

iOS 27 gave your iPhone an alarm feature that’s long been missing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.
  • Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm?
  • I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

iOS 27 has two upcoming sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a new volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

According to recent reports, do you initiative to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

Tech Report: Arctic: A Practical Lock-Free Adaptive Radix Tree

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Usenix

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newton Ni, Nicolas Garza, Jenny Stinehour, and Michael Goppert, The University of Texas at Austin; Michal Friedman, ETH Zürich; Emmett Witchel, The University of Texas at Austin.
  • Indexing data structures are vital to the modern systems ecosystem, but there are no indexes that offer high performance, lock freedom, and range scans.
  • OSDI '26 Open Access Sponsored byKing Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST).

Newton Ni, Nicolas Garza, Jenny Stinehour, and Michael Goppert, The University of Texas at Austin; Michal Friedman, ETH Zürich; Emmett Witchel, The University of Texas at Austin.

Indexing data structures are vital to the modern systems ecosystem, but there are no indexes that offer high performance, lock freedom, and range scans. Arctic is a lock-free adaptive radix tree that achieves all three: Arctic outcompetes lock-based indexes, including a concurrent hash map, on many YCSB configurations, guarantees non-blocking operation through careful metadata layout and an (eponymous) freezing-based coordination protocol, and offers non-linearizable range and prefix scans. Arctic also contributes a novel safe memory reclamation scheme that uses operation keys to approximate reachable pointers. We integrate Arctic into RocksDB and Turso, improving throughput up to 40% and 12% on their write-heavy benchmarks relative to their default skiplist indexes.

#165486. MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (708 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker states it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also swiftly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Industry observers note that qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

#165483. An anti-slavery sugar bowl (2024)

📅 28 Jun 2024 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1004 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ac ↗ Open Full Page

An anti-slavery sugar bowl (2024)

📅 28 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As part of ongoing efforts to patch the displays in our glass galleries, we are excited to put a very rare example of abolitionist glassware on public display for the first time in the main gallery (131).
  • The 18th-century vogue for tea and coffee created a frenzied demand for sugar, which bolstered the West Indian slave trade.
  • Sources indicate that anti-slavery domestic goods are an early example of ethical consumerism, which seeks change by appealing to the moral character of consumers and their peers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of ongoing efforts to patch the displays in our glass galleries, we are excited to put a very rare example of abolitionist glassware on public display for the first time in the main gallery (131). This glass sugar bowl, with its deep blue colour and gilt letters that read: East India Sugar, Not Made by Slaves, is a striking symbol of the abolitionist movement in Britain. It represents a complicated and violent chapter of British history in which sugar became inextricably linked with the slave trade. Its brilliant colour and gilt decoration are not diminished by the fact that it has been broken and was painstakingly repaired. Anti-slavery campaigners understood the influence that domestic goods had on British society and realised that by circulating their message on useful every-day items, they could inspire political change. Like the anti-slavery medallions produced by Wedgwood in the late 18th century, abolitionist sugar bowls were a tangible symbol of their owner’s political views.

The 18th-century vogue for tea and coffee created a frenzied demand for sugar, which bolstered the West Indian slave trade. Anti-slavery campaigners organised two crucial sugar boycotts in 1792-1793 and 1825-1829 with the intention of forcing parliament to halt the trafficking of enslaved people through the British Isles and to its colonies. These boycotts were spearheaded by Quakers and other abolitionists such as William Fox (active in the 1790s), who published An Address to the People of Great Britain, on the Utility of Refraining from the Use of West India Sugar and Rum. In this pamphlet, Fox draws graphic parallels between the consumption of sugar and cannibalism. His metaphor asserts that by partaking in a food that was directly linked to slavery, the consumer was no better than a cannibal. The Anti-Saccharites’ message was so successful that it is estimated approximately 300,000 people participated the sugar boycotts.

Sources indicate that anti-slavery domestic goods are an early example of ethical consumerism, which seeks change by appealing to the moral character of consumers and their peers. Abolitionists sought to juxtapose the violent horrors of slavery with the elegant and restrained ritual of drinking tea which had been so fervently appropriated by British women in the 18th-century. In doing so, anti-slavery campaigners succeeded in querying the moral and virtuous nature of wealthy and middle-class women. For these women, participating in the sugar boycotts was a political statement, which signalled their righteous character to their peers while also adhering to societal expectations. Not only did boycotting sugar become fashionable, but so too did abolitionist iconography on domestic goods. By quite literally serving up abolitionist ideas on their tea tables, gentlewomen were able to take part in politics as never before.

Recent findings suggest that although the Abolition of the Slave Trade Act of 1807 made it illegal to directly participate in the slave trade in British colonies, the West Indies still used forced labour to harvest and produce sugar. This triggered the second wave of sugar boycotts from 1825-1829, which was when the bowl in our collection was made.

It has been revealed that old advertisements tell us that other anti-slavery sugar bowls with similar slogans and decoration were produced and sold in England in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. However, these examples all appear to be ceramic rather than glass. An early 19th-century pamphlet tells us that Mrs. B. Henderson’s warehouse on Rye Lane, Peckham sold a variety of ceramic ‘East India Sugar Basins’ that read ‘East India Sugar Not Made by Slaves’ in gold lettering, very similar to the glass example in our collection. Recent research also suggests that some women’s abolitionist societies commissioned anti-slavery sugar tableware by well-known makers such as Herbert Minton, such as this jug in our collection, with profits going towards their cause.

Most known examples of abolitionist sugar bowls are ceramic and few of these survive today. The V&A sugar bowl is a very rare example made of glass and is possibly one of only two known to still exist, the other is held at the British Museum. It almost certainly originally had a lid, which has since been lost or destroyed. It was probably made in Bristol, which was an vital centre of glassmaking in Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries. Bristol and its port were also a significant leg of the transatlantic slave trade, which poured lots of money into the city, its industries and its inhabitants. While glassmakers may not have directly supported the slave trade, they certainly benefitted from it financially by selling sugar bowls, decanters and other goods that were intended for commodities harvested by enslaved peoples. It is, therefore, particularly significant that Bristol manufacturers who had historically benefited so greatly from the slave trade in the 18th century, also sought to benefit from the later sugar boycotts of the 1820s.

In a recent development, this glass sugar bowl represents a multifaceted and complicated era in Western history. The sugar boycotts were an influential protest that remind us that people have sought change through economic resistance for hundreds of years. Although anti-slavery goods successfully spread their message to a wider audience, we should be reminded that objects like this sugar bowl were a performative display of solidarity. White, middle- and upper-class people could display these objects while doing little else for the abolitionist cause. The absurdity of this performance is clearly felt when contrasting the decorous act of ‘taking tea’ sans sugar as a form of protest with the violence  to which enslaved people were subjected. Although the support of British people was imperative in the fight for abolition, we should not let this overshadow the conscious resistance initiated by enslaved people in securing their own freedom.

Next time you’re in the V&A do pay a visit to our glass galleries (Room 131) to see this rare example of abolitionist glassware. If you’re interested in learning more about abolitionist domestic goods ranging from anti-slavery medallions to handbags, come and see some examples that we hold in our collection.

10 stocks we like better than Tesla ›.

Humanoid robots grab people's attention as they walk on sidewalks. Granted, it's a rare sight since this technology is in its early stages, but there is plenty of excitement about the future.

In a recent development, while many start-ups are creating their own humanoid robots, it may be better for investors to invest in the companies selling shovels during a gold rush. Once hints of humanoid robotics leaders become more apparent and finances improve, it may be worth considering smaller companies.

For now, these three tech giants look well-positioned for the humanoid robot boom.

Image source: Agility Robotics.

Tesla (TSLA +11.46%) is the most direct, established American tech giant for exposure to humanoid robots. The company has been developing its Optimus robot segment for several years and has sufficient revenue and profits to ensure financial sustainability.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/23/26.

Recent findings suggest that revenue reached $28 billion in Q3, which was roughly flat year over year. The firm's "Services and other revenue" component was the only part of the business to grow, suggesting that Tesla's future growth will have to come from robots.

Net income wasn't as exciting, down 43% year over year, but $787 million in pure profit is still more impressive than humanoid robot start-up companies. While Tesla has been a volatile growth stock, it's actually one of the least-risky ways to gain exposure to humanoid robots. Tesla anticipates delivering orders in late 2027.

Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) isn't specifically a robotics stock, but its artificial intelligence chips are foundational for robotics. As demand for humanoid robots soars, Nvidia chips will gain even more traction. Grand View Research projects a 38.2% CAGR for the humanoid robot market through 2033, indicating the type of momentum Nvidia can ride.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/23/26.

While high demand for humanoid robots is critical to Tesla's long-term investment thesis, Nvidia continues to perform well in current times. Revenue surged 103% year over year in the manufacturer's fiscal 2027 third quarter, and its impressive guidance shows it is taking steps to gain market share.

Recent findings suggest that chief Financial Officer Colette Kress highlighted that the company's roadmap is on track and that demand is still booming. That's the type of news investors want to hear as 2026 comes to a close, and it further silences concerns about an AI bubble.

Meanwhile, AI stocks have been trending downward for several weeks. Fundamentals are still growing, but the best explanation may be concerns about higher rates and uncertainty with oil, even as the commodity's price continues to trend downward.

In any event, this sharp correction has produced an enticing valuation for Nvidia, making it cheaper than most S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.73%) stocks and putting it deep into value-stock territory.

Industry observers note that micron (MU +19.04%) plays a similar role to Nvidia in humanoid robots. They require vast amounts of memory to interact with the world and learn from their training, and Micron's chips fill in the gap.

Its technology will be part of the humanoid robot bedrock, and, like Nvidia, Micron isn't waiting for these robots to become mainstream before delivering compelling financial results.

Micron anticipates $61.5 billion in fiscal 2027 first-quarter revenue. That's more than a 4x increase from the $13.64 billion Micron generated in the same quarter last year. Micron has established a good reputation for beating the high end of its guidance throughout the AI boom, which makes a 5x growth rate possible.

Multi-year customer deals highlight the sustainability of the AI boom, but even with these bullish catalysts, Micron has been caught in the recent negative sentiment of the AI trade. It has a P/E ratio below 10, which offers an attractive entry point for investors who can wait out the current volatility.

Recent findings suggest that the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up….

In a recent development, the Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big revision last year, adding a variety of newly introduced higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

In a recent development, the Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a substantial patch over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”.

Sources indicate that with the latest system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The newly introduced sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean in Less Than 10 Years

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Phoronix

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This month brought the availability of the latest EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 Zen 6 server processors.
  • Sources indicate that the AMD EPYC 7601 launched back in June 2017 as the flagship of the EPYC Naples "Zen 1" processors.
  • Now just shy of a decade later, the EPYC 9006 SP7 processors have begun shipping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This month brought the availability of the latest EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 Zen 6 server processors. We have seen excellent generational gains with the likes of the EPYC 9686F and EPYC 9996 over Zen 5 Turin CPUs as well as sharply outperforming the competition from Intel and NVIDIA. With the first-generation EPYC "Naples" processors having launched nearly ten years ago, I was curious to quantify AMD's server performance gains over the past decade. So up today is a look at how the EPYC 9996 and EPYC 9686F Zen 6 processors compare to the original EPYC Zen 1 flagship with the EPYC 7601 across real-world workloads for performance as well as power efficiency for some pretty epic gains.

Sources indicate that the AMD EPYC 7601 launched back in June 2017 as the flagship of the EPYC Naples "Zen 1" processors. The EPYC 7601 was notable for its time with 32 x Zen 1 cores / 64 threads, 2.2GHz base frequency, 3.2GHz max boost frequency, and 64 MB of L3 cache. On the memory side was eight channel DDR4-2666 memory and for connectivity were up to 128 PCIe 3.0 lanes. The TDP of each EPYC 7601 processor is 180 Watts.

Now just shy of a decade later, the EPYC 9006 SP7 processors have begun shipping. With the AMD EPYC 9996 256-core flagship are 256 Zen 6C cores / 512 threads per socket, 2.55GHz base clock, 4.1GHz max boost frequency, and an incredible 1024MB of L3 cache. EPYC 9006 SP7 processors support DDR5 RDIMMs or up to MRDIMM-12800 memory at 16 channels. There is also 96 lanes of PCI Express 6.0. The EPYC 9996 has a 600W default power rating.

Or for the frequency-optimized flagship is the EPYC 9686F with 96 Zen 5 cores / 192 threads with a 4.05GHz base frequency and up to 5.3GHz maximum boost clock. The EPYC 9686F has a 384MB L3 cache size while also having a 600 Watt default power rating.

Over the past ten years of AMD EPYC there has been incredible architectural advancements too not reflected in the key specs alone such as AVX-512 with Zen 4 and further refined in Zen 5, security improvements to reduce the need for software-based security mitigations, and countless other architectural improvements each step of the way from Zen 1 to Zen 6.

It has been revealed that for comparing EPYC Zen 1 to Zen 6, I dusted off the Dell PowerEdge R7425 server originally provided by AMD for EPYC Naples testing at Phoronix. Nearly ten years later, the Dell PowerEdge server with the dual AMD EPYC 7601 processors still fires up and runs reliably. The AMD EPYC 7601 2P was running with 16 x 32GB DDR4-2666 memory, Samsung SSD 860 SSD storage, and other stock components of this Naples review unit.

With the AMD EPYC 9686F 2P and EPYC 9996 2P testing was the Nigeria reference server with 32 x 64GB MRDIMM-12800 memory, and Micron MTFDMBQ7T6THM-1BP1JABDC PCIe Gen6 SSD.

Sources indicate that the AMD EPYC Naples and EPYC Venice servers were tested on the same software stack with using Ubuntu 26.10 for a very up-to-date open-source software experience. Ubuntu 26.10 ships with the Linux 7.3 kernel and GCC 15.3 compiler by default.

Sources indicate that in addition to the raw performance testing for EPYC Zen 1 vs. EPYC Zen 6, the CPU power consumption and performance-per-Watt were also compared using the exposed CPU PowerCap/RAPL sensors of 2P processor configuration.

#165473. Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1847 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Stalw ↗ Open Full Page

Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Stalw

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook.
  • It has been revealed that stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover.
  • Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange.

It has been revealed that stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know.

Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL.

Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out.

Microsoft has not declared the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online:.

According to recent reports, none of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud.

In a recent development, for many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year.

Recent findings suggest that the obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client.

Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. Replacing Exchange with a standard IMAP and CalDAV server has always meant telling every one of those users to switch to a different mail client, or to reconfigure Outlook into a reduced IMAP mode where calendars and contacts no longer sync. For a migration project, that is often where the plan dies.

With Stalwart 1.2.0 the consumers do not need to change anything. The administrator moves the mailboxes and points the DNS records at Stalwart, and users connect with the same Outlook they used before.

Stalwart implements the following Microsoft protocols, all served on the same HTTPS port as JMAP and the WebUI:.

That set of protocols is what the following clients use to talk to an Exchange server, and they can connect to Stalwart the same way:.

The Exchange protocols are not a separate silo inside Stalwart. They are another door into the same accounts. A message filed in Outlook is in the same mailbox an IMAP or JMAP client sees, a meeting accepted on a phone appears in the calendar that CalDAV clients read, and a contact added in Apple Contacts shows up in the CardDAV address book. A user can keep Outlook on the office desktop, the native mail app on a phone and a JMAP webmail in the browser, all on one account.

Recent findings suggest that rules created in Outlook’s Rules and Alerts are stored on the server as mail rules, which run as Sieve when the message is delivered. They apply when Outlook is closed and whatever client the user opens next. Delegates and folder permissions set in Outlook become regular Stalwart shares, so they apply to every protocol. Shared mailboxes open automatically in Outlook from group membership, as they do with Exchange.

Not every part of an Exchange deployment has a counterpart. Stalwart does not offer public folders, archive mailboxes, mobile device management, RPC over HTTP (Outlook 2010 and earlier) or NTLM and Kerberos sign-in: clients authenticate with a password, an app password or OAuth. The Exchange documentation covers configuration, DNS and Autodiscover, each family of clients, and the differences from Exchange that administrators should know about before a migration.

One Outlook is missing from the list above: the latest Outlook for Windows, the one that Windows now installs by default and that classic Outlook keeps offering through a toggle in its title bar.

The new Outlook does not work with Stalwart, and it does not work with any self-hosted server, Exchange included. It is built to work through Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft does not support on-premises Exchange accounts in it at all.

It has been revealed that the upcoming Outlook does accept IMAP accounts, and that might look like a way around the problem. It is not. When an IMAP account is added to the new Outlook, the connection to the mail server is not made from the user’s computer. As heise and c’t reported in November 2023, the new Outlook sends the IMAP server name, the user name and the password to Microsoft, and Microsoft’s cloud connects to the mail server on the user’s behalf. Every message then passes through Microsoft’s infrastructure on its way to the screen. Microsoft does not only see the mail; it holds the password to the mailbox.

For an organisation that runs its own mail server to keep its data under its own control, this defeats the purpose of the whole exercise. We advise against using the new Outlook with any self-hosted email deployment, whether it runs Stalwart or anything else. Users who see the “Try the new Outlook” toggle in classic Outlook should leave it off.

The same applies on phones. Outlook for iOS and Android reach on-premises mailboxes through a Microsoft cloud service as well, which requires a hybrid Exchange Online setup. On mobile devices, the native mail, calendar and contacts apps, which connect directly over ActiveSync, are the better choice.

According to recent reports, the obvious question is why Stalwart is adding Exchange protocols now. EWS is being removed from Exchange Online, Microsoft’s own future for Outlook is a cloud client, and classic Outlook is reportedly supported until 2029. Why build support for protocols that will be obsolete in a few years?

Because the companies that run Exchange today cannot wait a few years, and because those protocols are the bridge they need to cross.

It has been revealed that an organisation with a few hundred Outlook users cannot replace its mail server and its mail client in the same weekend. It can replace the server, though, if nobody notices. With Stalwart speaking the Exchange protocols, the server moves first: mailboxes are migrated, DNS records change, and on Monday every user opens the same Outlook and the same phone apps they used on Friday. The organisation’s mail is back under its own control from day one, and no one’s work is interrupted to get there.

Recent findings suggest that the client can then change at the pace that suits the customers. Over time, as classic Outlook reaches the end of its life and the new Outlook remains tied to Microsoft’s cloud, we expect users to move gradually to third-party email clients built on open standards, and in particular on JMAP. Outlook will stop being an option for anyone who cares about where their email lives, and by then the people who used it will have had the time to choose something else without a deadline over their heads.

Exchange support is not where Stalwart is going. It is how organisations get from where they are to where Stalwart is.

Exchange compatibility is not a small piece of work. It adds about 200,000 lines of code to Stalwart, and we know that some of you would rather not carry that weight if you never plan to see an Outlook client. We built it with that in mind, so that it costs as little as possible for those who do not use it, and so that it can be removed cleanly once the Exchange protocols are obsolete:.

A drop-in replacement is only useful if the data can follow. Vandelay, our account import and export tool, migrates mailboxes from both sides of Microsoft’s offering:.

Vandelay copies each account into Stalwart over JMAP, and the domain moves to Stalwart when its MX records and client settings change. The migration guide for hosted services walks through the whole process, from the first test account to the cutover. With the Exchange protocols enabled on Stalwart, Outlook and the other Exchange clients then connect through Autodiscover and find the migrated mail, calendars and contacts.

Exchange support is the headline, but 1.2.0 brings several other features, most of them developed alongside it because an Exchange replacement needs them:.

The changelog lists every change and fix, along with the upgrade steps: existing servers need to add the upcoming permissions to their default roles.

Industry observers note that last week we also released version 2.0.0 of stalwart-cli, and its biggest addition is an interactive console. Run stalwart-cli with no arguments in a terminal and it opens a full-screen interface that covers the same ground as the WebUI: browsing and editing accounts, domains and every other configuration object, watching the dashboard, following live traces and running actions. It is aimed at administrators who live in SSH sessions, or who work on hosts where opening a browser is impractical.

Industry observers note that the console is built with Ratatui, the excellent Rust library for terminal user interfaces, and it is schema-driven like the rest of the CLI: its screens, forms and field help come from the schema that the server publishes, so it picks up upcoming objects without being updated. The CLI also learned to sign in with the OAuth device flow and to remember the session, so a single approval in the browser is enough for both the console and every subsequent command.

It has been revealed that stalwart will be at FOSDEM 2027 in Brussels. We will have a Stalwart stand, and on Saturday, 30 January 2027, we will give a talk about moving from Microsoft Exchange to Stalwart in the Modern Email devroom. If you are planning a migration away from Exchange, or are curious about what it takes, come and talk to us. We will post the time and title of the talk once the schedule is published.

Until then, the Exchange documentation has everything needed to try it, and we would love to hear how your Outlook clients get on with Stalwart.

According to recent reports, if you’re comparing hotels for a weekend trip, for example, ChatGPT can weigh a shorter walk against a lower nightly rate. It can also offer to alert you when something you’re shopping for drops in price.

The global rollout starts today for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise people.

As for the outgoing models, OpenAI says it will retire GPT-5.6 Sol from Chat, Work, and Codex on December 23.

GPT-5.6 Terra will also leave ChatGPT Work and Codex on the same day next month.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andreas Kling — Mon, 23 Nov 2026.

In a recent development, hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^).

Recent findings suggest that ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the matter with its latest Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software revision adds the following:.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

It has been revealed that synthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

#165467. Worshipping at the Altar of Brendan Gregg

Worshipping at the Altar of Brendan Gregg

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fzakaria

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI.
  • In a recent development, I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables.
  • Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

In a recent development, I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

In a recent development, the critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

It has been revealed that if you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲.

I added a newly introduced rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod!

Sources indicate that aside: Fresh to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

According to recent reports, let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

Sources indicate that the usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤.

Every rewind time starts with two numbers:.

The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

Industry observers note that the line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.

In a recent development, A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤.

Here is the whole output for libuv:.

Recent findings suggest that the second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path.22A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief.

In this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests, libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.

According to recent reports, all of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.

Drag can be less than time on the path.

The last table answers a different question: how much sooner would the run finish if this part took no time? The critical path method calls this drag.

For the truly magical part, we can jump to any part of the path and see what was happening, invoke gdb and fork the run at that moment. A profiler hands you a stack, sampled at some moment you can never go back to. Every frame in rewind time is a moment in a recording, and Rewind can replay the run to it.

--in looks inside one process,33It can take a pid, a program or a word of the command line. so let’s dive into the hrtime test that spent 3.38 seconds asleep in clock_nanosleep:.

Since this test spent 100% of its time asleep, the step provided on the last line is where it began. rewind where replays the run to that step and asks gdb where the thread was:.

It has been revealed that 🎯 We can see that the test is calling uv_sleep(45) from line 39 of test/test-hrtime.c, and that it is sleeping for 45 milliseconds. It does that 75 times for a total of 3.38 seconds.44Turns out that the test sleeps on purpose: it is checking how far uv_hrtime moves across a sleep. There is nothing to optimize in this case.

As the cherry on top: the run is deterministic, so step 115,894 is the same instruction every time you replay it. You can open rewind gdb at that step and investigate to your heart’s content.

According to recent reports, the Rewind app’s Time tab indicates the same answers. The path becomes a flame graph, colored the way Gregg colors his off-CPU flame graphs: computing is warm, asleep is blue, and a process shades from one to the other by how much of its time it slept.

In a recent development, clicking a frame picks it and moves the playhead there, so the build log, the process tree and the files all show that moment; clicking a process again zooms into it. When you pick a blue frame, the app replays the run to that part’s longest sleep and demonstrates the stack where it slept:.

Under the stack, Show source opens the source panel at that moment on that thread, and Open gdb here opens gdb in a fork of the run at the sleep:.

If you’d rather use tools you already know, rewind time can emit the data in their formats: folded stacks for flamegraph.pl and speedscope, or a Perfetto trace for ui.perfetto.dev.

The flame graph below is the real flamegraph.pl output: click a frame to zoom in, or open it on its own.

Sources indicate that every idea here predates Rewind. Gregg has been drawing off-CPU and wakeup flame graphs for over a decade, and build systems have reported critical path information potentially even longer.55Bazel’s critical path analysis is a great example of this, and it has been around for years. I have been inspired by his work since I first dabbled in eBPF, back when flame graphs were new. 🙇.

Recent findings suggest that what Rewind adds is the data. Lots of it.

Sources indicate that rewind has that data because it can’t replay without it. On a single CPU the only thing that changes from run to run is the scheduler, so every recording already logs every context switch.

This changes the economics of performance analysis. On a live machine, you have to trace before the run, and tracing has a cost. You can only trace a few runs, and you have to pick which ones. Rewind traces every run, so you can analyze any of them later, and do so exactly.

It has just been a manic fever joy to take ideas I have admired for years, point them at a deterministic VM, and watch them work in ways that are hard or impossible on a normal machine.

Please accept rewind time as my offering at the altar of Brendan Gregg.
